title: HuluOPD: Unifying Heterogeneous Medical Specialists into One Lightweight Model with Unlabeled Prompts
abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.

title: An Automated Framework Integrating Deep Learning and Anatomical Reasoning for Cardiac Phenotyping From CCTA
abstract: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) depicts coronary anatomy and cardiac fat, but segmentation alone does not ensure anatomically consistent measurements. We propose an automated framework that combines deep learning with anatomical reasoning for quantitative cardiac phenotyping. Its anatomical measurement module uses graph geometry, branch identity, and surrounding structures to define vessel-specific pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) sampling and a surrogate epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) compartment. The latter also generates training targets without requiring expert pericardium contours. A companion module quantifies coronary calcium on non-contrast CT. Component-wise benchmarking was conducted on five public datasets: ImageCAS, ImageCAS-X, COCA, Visual Lab, and MultiD4CAD. On ImageCAS-X Test-160, lumen segmentation with validation-selected post-processing achieved a Dice score of 0.9133 and a clDice score of 0.940, exceeding the corresponding published CAS-Net point estimates. In the four-split ImageCAS evaluation, the four-member ensemble outperformed the single ResEnc-L model. Analysis of 800 paired scans showed that PCAT attenuation measurements differed between whole-vessel and lumen references. External EAT evaluation showed strong volume correlation and good spatial overlap. Explicit anatomical rules make the resulting measurements interpretable and inspectable. In practice, the framework provides a standardized pipeline for processing cardiac CT cohorts and quantifying coronary calcium, PCAT, and EAT for population-level analysis and comparison across studies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/HarryTRAN207/CardiacCT-Research

title: Interpretable Orthogonal Latent Diffusion with Scale-Selective Uncertainty for Medical Image Super-Resolution
abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used for medical image reconstruction and super-resolution, but their samples may contain plausible fine-scale hallucinations that are difficult to identify from the reconstructed image alone. We propose Med-PODiff, a patch-wise proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) diffusion framework for brain MRI super-resolution that performs generative reconstruction in compact and interpretable local coefficient spaces. Unlike pixel-space or learned-latent diffusion models, Med-PODiff uses the POD structure to separate low-rank anatomical variation from fine-detail residual variation, enabling predictive uncertainty to be decomposed into total, coarse, and fine components. Building on this decomposition, we define a pixel-wise hallucination-risk score, $H_p$, that emphasizes regions where fine-detail uncertainty dominates coarse structural uncertainty. On brain MRI, Med-PODiff outperforms representative diffusion baselines in reconstruction quality while producing well-calibrated predictive intervals, with total uncertainty detecting high-error regions at AUROC 0.954. More importantly, the decomposed uncertainty is scale-selective: coarse and fine uncertainty preferentially predict errors at the corresponding scales, with $H_p$ localizing fine error at AUROC $0.906$. Controlled injections and retrospective Cartesian $k$-space undersampling further support fine-detail localization and degradation robustness. The discarded POD tail is only $3.8\%$ of the retained fine-error magnitude, and Med-PODiff improves downstream segmentation consistency while requiring substantially less inference time than pixel-space diffusion.

title: CSC-Mamba: Bridging multimodal convolutional sparse coding and state space models for multi-contrast MRI super-resolution
abstract: Multi-contrast MRI super-resolution accelerates clinical protocols by reconstructing high-resolution (HR) target modalities from low-resolution (LR) inputs, guided by easily acquired reference contrasts. While purely data-driven deep neural networks achieve strong performance via rich representation capacity, they rely on heuristic fusion mechanisms (e.g., naive concatenation or black-box cross-attention) that lack theoretical grounding. Alternatively, model-based deep unfolding networks enforce principled cross-contrast fusion through explicit priors, yet their unrolled steps remain constrained to shallow convolutions, lacking modern deep blocks to capture global context. To bridge this gap, we propose CSC-MAMBA, unifying deep-unfolded multimodal convolutional sparse coding with the Vision Mamba state-space backbone. By fusing common structural priors from the guidance modality via unfolded sparse coding and globally refining contrast-specific representations with a Mamba back- bone, our approach benefits from interpretable, model-guided fusion and long-range spatial context. Experiments on the IXI dataset demonstrate that CSC-MAMBA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction quality, achieving up to a 0.62 dB gain in PSNR while remaining computationally efficient.

title: FlashSegmentator: High-Throughput TotalSegmentator Inference without Loss of Accuracy
abstract: Purpose: To develop, evaluate, and publicly release FlashSegmentator, an open-source inference pipeline that increases the throughput of TotalSegmentator without retraining or loss of segmentation accuracy. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study used public datasets: 73 CT examinations from the TotalSegmentator test split (median age, 65 years; 37 male, 35 female, one unknown), 30 abdominal CT examinations from the Beyond the Cranial Vault (BTCV) dataset, 512 training-split CT examinations for concurrent-process analysis, and 55 MRI examinations. FlashSegmentator adds static-shape compilation, pipelining, batched sliding-window inference, and GPU postprocessing. Throughput was compared with the reference implementation (including its lower-resolution modes) and FastSegmentator on GH200, A100, and T4 GPUs. Dice agreement was tested with two one-sided tests (margin, +/-0.01). Results: FlashSegmentator processed 3782, 1810, and 270 examinations per hour on the GH200, A100, and T4 (57.7, 33.9, and 6.4 times the reference implementation and 3.20, 2.50, and 1.22 times compiled FastSegmentator). Dice scores were equivalent for all 117 structures on every GPU (mean difference <= 1.2 x 10^-5; P < .001) and at the examination level on BTCV. In contrast, the lower-resolution modes of the reference implementation processed 181 and 213 examinations per hour on the A100 but reduced mean Dice by 0.116 and 0.241. On MRI, throughput increased 94-fold with all 50 structures equivalent. Estimated A100 cloud cost per 10,000 examinations decreased from 997 to 29 US dollars. Conclusion: FlashSegmentator increased the throughput of TotalSegmentator on data center and entry-level GPUs without loss of segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation.

title: DiCT: Teaching X-ray Vision-Language Models to Reason via Imagining CT
abstract: Diagnosing with X-rays often requires reasoning about the 3D locations of abnormalities and their spatial relationships to surrounding anatomical structures, yet such reasoning remains challenging due to the loss of spatial information in 2D projections. To address this challenge, we propose Dreaming in CT (DiCT), a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that leverages a CT vision-language model (VLM) to guide an X-ray VLM. Through this CT-guided transfer, the student acquires CT-informed 3D reasoning capabilities, enabling it to reason directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference time. The framework begins with instruct the dreamer, which equips the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning capabilities and establishes a structured interface that distinguishes X-ray observations from CT imagination. Building on this structure, visualize the dream introduces CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD), where the CT teacher selectively guides the X-ray student's reasoning trajectories to transfer 3D anatomical knowledge. Finally, manifest the dream adapts the acquired reasoning capabilities from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. Experiments across two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA demonstrate DiCT's effectiveness across radiological reasoning tasks, achieving a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77$\times$ lower inference computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongYep/DiCT.

title: Characterizing Datasets to Anticipate Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Performance for Radiographic Pneumonia Detection
abstract: Deep learning models for pneumonia detection from chest radiographs exhibit degraded accuracy when applied across institutions, which motivates Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA). We observe that UDA performance depends on the properties of both the source and target datasets, and that performance gains are asymmetric with respect to dataset pairs. We investigate which structural properties of chest X-ray datasets are the most important predictors of UDA performance, and whether they can be measured before adaptation is attempted. Five chest radiograph datasets were characterized by the class separability of their features, obtained from one forward pass of a frozen DenseNet-121 and summarized by the Silhouette Score, with the Fisher Ratio as a supporting measure. All twenty directed source-target pairs were adapted with a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN), while direct transfer without adaptation was also evaluated. Seven published transferability estimators were computed on the same representation for comparison. We found that adaptation performance depended on both endpoints in opposite directions. More separable target datasets attained higher AUC scores ($r=0.934$, $p=0.042$), whereas more separable sources produced lower AUC scores ($r=-0.922$, $p=0.017$). The signed difference in separability tracked the signed difference in AUC between the two directions of a pair ($r=-0.932$, $p=0.017$) and identified the better direction in 10 of 10 pairs ($p=0.001$). The proposed descriptor was comparable to the best published estimators on target evaluation. Source and target datasets play opposite structural roles in adaptation: higher class separability makes a dataset easier as a test set but not as a training source. This framework can guide dataset selection for adaptation in low-resource settings without running full experiments.

title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

title: Adaptive and Detection-Aware Super-Resolution for Small Object Detection
abstract: Image super-resolution aims to reconstruct a high-resolution image from a low-resolution input and is relevant for surveillance, satellite imagery, medical imaging, and object detection. This paper investigates SRCNN-based single-image super-resolution for a scale factor of x4, starting from a classical baseline and progressively introducing residual learning, Charbonnier loss, and adaptive loss functions. The proposed approach includes a three-region adaptive loss, where image areas are divided into smooth, texture, and edge regions using gradient information. The models are evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and EdgeMAE in order to measure both reconstruction quality and structural detail preservation. In addition to reconstruction evaluation, the paper analyzes the impact of super-resolution on object detection. A YOLOv8 detector is applied to images processed through bicubic interpolation and SRCNN-based variants, using images from the COCO validation dataset. The results show that improved reconstruction quality does not always lead to better detection performance. However, for small objects, a detection-aware variant combined with residual scaling improves the F1 score compared to the bicubic baseline. These results highlight the importance of task-aware evaluation when super-resolution is used in computer vision pipelines.

title: GeoSurge: Geometry-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning for Auditable Liver Resection Planning
abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.

title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.

title: IMPACT-Seg: Consistent Anatomical Segmentation and Representation Learning Across CT, CBCT, and MRI
abstract: Computed tomography (CT), cone-beam CT (CBCT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide complementary representations of the same underlying anatomy, yet substantial differences in image appearance challenge consistent segmentation and deformable registration in adaptive radiotherapy. We investigate whether dense anatomical segmentation supervision can promote cross-modality correspondence without explicit feature alignment. We introduce IMPACT-Seg, which segments 126 structures across CT, CBCT, and MRI using shared network parameters. A collection of 8,290 volumes was assembled from public cohorts through label harmonization, model-assisted pseudo-label completion, iterative refinement, and 2,864 physics-based CBCT simulations with voxel-aligned CT labels. Unpaired images were used to jointly train 2.5D and 3D residual-encoder networks. On 139 real CBCTs, IMPACT-Seg 3D achieved a mean Dice of 0.842 versus 0.671 for the strongest comparator. On 497 voxel-aligned CT-simulated-CBCT pairs, the CT-to-CBCT Dice decrease was 0.022 versus 0.153-0.178 for competing methods. On independent pancreatic radiotherapy CBCTs, gastrointestinal Dice was 0.735 versus 0.634 for TotalSegmentator. Prediction agreement reached 0.881 on registered CT-CBCT and 0.790 on CT-MRI pairs. Adding MRI training data reduced CT-MRI encoder feature retrieval error from 36.8 to 3.2 mm. Registration pipelines incorporating IMPACT-Seg features ranked first on two multimodal Learn2Reg benchmarks. The 3D model segmented a whole-body CT in 15 s. These findings show that dense anatomical segmentation supervision can support consistent anatomical representations across modalities, with applications to both segmentation and registration. Code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/HEMONCedric/IMPACTSeg.

title: FedTumor-IoMT: Federated Learning-Aided Brain Tumor Diagnosis on Resource-Constrained Edge IoMT Devices
abstract: Joint brain tumor segmentation and classification models are computationally intensive, limiting their training on resource-constrained edge platforms and restricting privacy-preserving Federated Learning FL in the Internet of Medical Things IoMT. Existing approaches either perform both tasks on GPU-equipped workstations or support only classification on edge devices. To address this gap, this work proposes a lightweight multitask FL framework for joint segmentation and classification through local edge training. A shared pretrained LiteMedSAM encoder with TinyViT extracts features for a coordinate-attention-based segmentation decoder and a segmentation-guided classification head, eliminating a separate feature extractor. Selective encoder freezing retains 95\% trainable parameters while reducing on-device training costs. The proposed framework is experimentally validated on a laboratory testbed of five resource-constrained edge clients using 1,200 T1-weighted MRI samples. It achieves 94.20\% classification accuracy, 88.53\% DSC, 83.68\% IoU, and 99.87\% ROC-AUC. Its classification accuracy remains within 0.6\% of the GPU-trained baseline of 95.21\% across five FL rounds. The attention and feature refinement modules improve DSC and IoU by 3.82\% and 4.60\%, respectively, with 0.74 GFLOPs of additional computation. On edge hardware, the framework achieves 46.54 s inference latency, 52.8\% CPU utilization, and a peak temperature of 65$^\circ$C without thermal throttling. Its inference latency is observed to be 6.4--10.5 times lower than that of existing frameworks. These results demonstrate the feasibility of privacy-preserving joint brain tumor segmentation and classification on resource-constrained edge platforms.

title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains
abstract: Local queries of a Markov chain can depend on past updates outside the queried components. For pseudo-marginal chains with Gaussian graph priors, we construct decision certificates from finite historical parameter ranges to settle updates before all neighbouring records are resolved. Under shared random inputs and exact arithmetic, the executor recovers the reference parameters, auxiliary variables and likelihood estimates for any prespecified finite query sequence. We bound conditional expected work, including likelihood evaluation, historical range construction and execution management. On specified path and grid families, we fix per-node history lengths and all other parameters in the work bounds. As graph size grows, expected incremental work stays bounded for certificate execution and grows linearly for the specified cached pointwise evaluator answering the same query. In controlled experiments, certificate execution is faster than pointwise and parallel Picard execution for sparse queries, whereas Picard is faster than certificate execution for full queries. We apply the method to positron emission tomography and Gaussian process classification of Landmine data. For a fixed numerical tomography posterior, certificate execution completes all queries of regional mean distribution volume within budget, while full execution completes none from the same initial cache. In Landmine, posterior summaries of the difference in log length scales between two sites agree across pseudo-marginal and ancillary augmentation samplers within estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. Certificate execution resolves almost every scheduled update over the full query sequence.

title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration
abstract: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/

title: SUPRA: Synthesizing Amyloid PET from MRI and Plasma Biomarkers with an Explicit Regional SUVR Prior
abstract: Amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) quantifies brain amyloid-$β$ as a standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR), but is costly and not widely available. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is routine, and plasma biomarkers such as phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) are becoming practical. Synthesizing amyloid PET from MRI alone is ill-posed, because brain anatomy reveals little about amyloid burden. We present SUPRA (SUVR prior-guided amyloid synthesis), which divides this task between MRI and plasma biomarkers. A regression maps the plasma panel to regional SUVR levels, painted onto the subject's MRI segmentation as an explicit prior. A 3D network then adds a residual correction guided by MRI. The output is in absolute SUVR, and the model also runs on p-tau217 alone. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort (111 test pairs), SUPRA reaches a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 23.4 dB, against at most 20.7 dB for four published models, and rank correlations of 0.56 to 0.67 with true SUVR in the composite cortex, an early-accumulation region and the striatum, against at most 0.24. In a second, cognitively unimpaired cohort with other plasma platforms (143 test pairs), it reaches 22.8 dB and 0.32 to 0.61, against at most 21.4 dB and 0.20. Its area under the curve for amyloid positivity is 0.91 and 0.82, against at most 0.63. Ablations show that plasma supplies the amyloid information and the network the image quality. Combining MRI with a blood test yields synthetic amyloid PET that is realistic and tracks burden across regions.

title: DDxBasis: Explaining Frozen Foundation Encoder-based Medical Classification by Exact Differential Diagnosis
abstract: In differential diagnosis (DDx), a clinician explains a diagnosis by the few findings that separate it from the alternatives. Medical image classifiers cannot yet explain themselves this way. Existing explanations are either faithful but spread over hundreds of concepts, or compact but leave part of each decision unexplained. We present DDxBasis, which explains a classifier on a frozen foundation encoder as a differential diagnosis in three steps. First, a concept bottleneck reads all patch tokens at every encoder layer using gated, second-order slot attention. A concept basis then regroups the concepts into two-pole axes, each a differential between groups of diagnoses. Finally, we read a differential diagnosis from each axis through the typical presentation of its poles, the pertinent findings of the case, and counterfactual edits of borderline cases. Across five medical datasets, DDxBasis is the most accurate frozen-encoder model and close to the best published domain-specific results. Because every concept adds its own evidence, its reproducible concept basis splits each decision exactly, at no cost in accuracy. Without ordered stage or concept labels, the axes recover cell lineages and rare subtypes, agree with dermatologists' structure annotations, and expose planted and real shortcuts.

title: Anatomy-Aware Pseudo-Labels and Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff Supervision for Semi-Supervised Pancreas Segmentation
abstract: Confidence-gated co-training assumes that pseudo-label errors are uncertain and concentrated at organ boundaries. We argue that for pancreas CT, where the target organ is a single connected structure and detached fragments are anatomically implausible, the dominant failures arise at three levels: where the organ is, what its boundary should look like, and how a correct boundary is penalized. Anatomical Rectification relabels implausible fragments of a teacher prediction as confident background, without adding any loss or parameter; an audit confirms that its rejections are overwhelmingly detached hallucinations and that thin, tail-like slices are not eroded. Boundary Grafting transplants labelled surface regions with their annotation into unlabeled volumes, replacing unreliable boundary pseudo-labels with ground truth. The residual error is coherent surface displacement, weakly penalized by permutation-invariant Dice and cross-entropy losses. Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff (HAH) supervision anneals a distance-weighted penalty from an annotation-anchored objective that is convex in the prediction to a Hausdorff surrogate, admitting the prediction-dependent distance term only after the predicted surface becomes reliable. On NIH pancreas CT, under the standard semi-supervised split, the full method reaches 84.60% Dice and 4.97 voxels 95HD, improving all four metrics over compared methods; on MSD Task07, 78.90% Dice and 4.19 voxels 95HD. We further contribute PanTS-SSL, a semi-supervised evaluation protocol derived from the public 9,901-case PanTS corpus, with a curated 1,015-volume main pool, labelled tiers of 50, 100 and 250 volumes, an 80-case tumor track, shift probes for acquisition and anatomy change, and a fixed 901-volume test set. On it, the method exceeds the co-training baseline at 100 labels, scales to 85.29% Dice at 250 labels, and reaches 85.50% Dice at 100 labels with HAH.

title: PICE: Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution Toward Self-Evolving Medical Image Recognition
abstract: Medical image classifiers in clinical practice must continually evolve to accommodate emerging disease categories while maintaining reliable classification of existing conditions. This is challenging because privacy and data-sharing restrictions limit access to historical patient data, while assigning dedicated capacity to each new diagnostic task causes linear model growth. Effective evolution requires preserving prior disease knowledge without retaining historical images while expanding model capacity only when necessary. To this end, we propose PICE, a Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution framework organized around what to preserve, when evolution is needed, and how that evolution is realized. PICE preserves prior disease knowledge in a prototype-statistical memory. For each incoming task, it assesses compatibility with historical references reconstructed from memory, reusing the closest adapter when compatibility is sufficient and instantiating a new one when evolution is required. PICE then realizes evolution by updating the memory and recalibrating the unified classifier with Gaussian pseudo features, thereby integrating new knowledge into the cumulative diagnostic space. During inference, memory-derived similarities guide task-agnostic adapter selection and fusion, enabling prediction over all learned disease categories. Experiments on Skin8, Kvasir-V2, and Path16 demonstrate the effectiveness of PICE across diverse clinical scenarios. On Skin8, PICE achieves a 7.60\% improvement in accuracy over the SOTA method on new tasks, while maintaining 71.10\% accuracy on previous tasks. It also reduces additional learnable parameters by 18.51\%. These results indicate that PICE improves classification while balancing knowledge retention, adaptation, and parameter growth, supporting continual model evolution as new diagnostic categories emerge without access to historical images.

title: A Plasma eMTBR-Tau Immunoassay for Detection of Advanced Insoluble Tau Pathology.
abstract: Importance Blood biomarkers that reflect neurofibrillary tau burden, a defining hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD), remain limited. Endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau 243 (eMTBR-tau243) has shown promise when measured by mass spectrometry; a scalable immunoassay could broaden research access and support clinical evaluation. Objective To determine whether plasma levels of eMTBR-tau measured by a novel immunoassay are associated with tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology defined by neuropathology and tau positron emission tomography (PET). Design, setting, and participants This cross-sectional study included brain donors with antemortem plasma from 2 US autopsy cohorts, and individuals with plasma samples and tau PET from 2 imaging cohorts in Canada and Sweden, with visits between 2002 and 2025 depending on the cohort. Exposures Plasma eMTBR-tau measured with an immunoassay and eMTBR-tau243 measured with mass spectrometry. Main outcomes and measures Plasma eMTBR-tau levels across neuropathologic Braak neurofibrillary tangle stages (I-VI, ranging from tangles confined to the entorhinal region to widespread neocortical tangles) and tau-PET Braak stages (0-VI), expressed as fold changes. Correlations with regional tau-PET standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs; higher values indicating more tau tangles), discrimination of regional tau-PET positivity (area under the curve [AUC]), and correlation with mass spectrometry-based eMTBR-tau243. Results The study included 728 participants in 4 cohorts (median age by cohort, 71.0-83.5 years; 41.3%-56.6% female). In the 2 autopsy cohorts (n = 241 and n = 240), eMTBR-tau age- and sex-adjusted geometric means were 0.0021 pg/mL and 0.0040 pg/mL, respectively, at Braak stages I-II vs 0.107 pg/mL and 0.101 pg/mL at Braak stage VI (50.5-fold [95% CI, 26.3-97.0] and 25.2-fold [95% CI, 15.8-40.3] higher for stage VI vs stages I-II; P < .001 for both cohorts). In one imaging cohort (n = 99), compared with tau-PET Braak stage 0, eMTBR-tau levels were 11.0-fold (95% CI, 6.9-17.5) higher at stages III-IV and 59.9-fold (95% CI, 39.5-90.7) higher at stages V-VI. Among participants positive for amyloid-β (Aβ) in another imaging cohort (n = 50), the Spearman rank correlations for eMTBR-tau with tau-PET SUVRs were ρ = 0.52 (95% CI, 0.28-0.70) in Braak regions I-II, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.61-0.86) in regions III-IV, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.75-0.91) in regions V-VI (all P < .001). Immunoassay and mass spectrometry measurements were strongly correlated (Spearman rank correlation, ρ = 0.93 in all participants [n = 108] and ρ = 0.96 in Aβ-positive participants [n = 54]) and discriminated tau-PET positivity similarly (n = 102; AUC range, 0.96-0.99 for the immunoassay and 0.97-0.99 for mass spectrometry). Conclusions and relevance A plasma eMTBR-tau immunoassay identified neocortical tau pathology in autopsy and tau-PET cohorts and correlated strongly with mass spectrometry measurements, a proof of principle that eMTBR-tau can be measured by immunoassay as a marker of advanced neurofibrillary tangle pathology.

Importance

Blood biomarkers that reflect neurofibrillary tau burden, a defining hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD), remain limited. Endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region tau 243 (eMTBR-tau243) has shown promise when measured by mass spectrometry; a scalable immunoassay could broaden research access and support clinical evaluation.

Objective

To determine whether plasma levels of eMTBR-tau measured by a novel immunoassay are associated with tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology defined by neuropathology and tau positron emission tomography (PET).

Design, setting, and participants

This cross-sectional study included brain donors with antemortem plasma from 2 US autopsy cohorts, and individuals with plasma samples and tau PET from 2 imaging cohorts in Canada and Sweden, with visits between 2002 and 2025 depending on the cohort.

Exposures

Plasma eMTBR-tau measured with an immunoassay and eMTBR-tau243 measured with mass spectrometry.

Main outcomes and measures

Plasma eMTBR-tau levels across neuropathologic Braak neurofibrillary tangle stages (I-VI, ranging from tangles confined to the entorhinal region to widespread neocortical tangles) and tau-PET Braak stages (0-VI), expressed as fold changes. Correlations with regional tau-PET standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs; higher values indicating more tau tangles), discrimination of regional tau-PET positivity (area under the curve [AUC]), and correlation with mass spectrometry-based eMTBR-tau243.

Results

The study included 728 participants in 4 cohorts (median age by cohort, 71.0-83.5 years; 41.3%-56.6% female). In the 2 autopsy cohorts (n = 241 and n = 240), eMTBR-tau age- and sex-adjusted geometric means were 0.0021 pg/mL and 0.0040 pg/mL, respectively, at Braak stages I-II vs 0.107 pg/mL and 0.101 pg/mL at Braak stage VI (50.5-fold [95% CI, 26.3-97.0] and 25.2-fold [95% CI, 15.8-40.3] higher for stage VI vs stages I-II; P < .001 for both cohorts). In one imaging cohort (n = 99), compared with tau-PET Braak stage 0, eMTBR-tau levels were 11.0-fold (95% CI, 6.9-17.5) higher at stages III-IV and 59.9-fold (95% CI, 39.5-90.7) higher at stages V-VI. Among participants positive for amyloid-β (Aβ) in another imaging cohort (n = 50), the Spearman rank correlations for eMTBR-tau with tau-PET SUVRs were ρ = 0.52 (95% CI, 0.28-0.70) in Braak regions I-II, 0.76 (95% CI, 0.61-0.86) in regions III-IV, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.75-0.91) in regions V-VI (all P < .001). Immunoassay and mass spectrometry measurements were strongly correlated (Spearman rank correlation, ρ = 0.93 in all participants [n = 108] and ρ = 0.96 in Aβ-positive participants [n = 54]) and discriminated tau-PET positivity similarly (n = 102; AUC range, 0.96-0.99 for the immunoassay and 0.97-0.99 for mass spectrometry).

Conclusions and relevance

A plasma eMTBR-tau immunoassay identified neocortical tau pathology in autopsy and tau-PET cohorts and correlated strongly with mass spectrometry measurements, a proof of principle that eMTBR-tau can be measured by immunoassay as a marker of advanced neurofibrillary tangle pathology.

title: Assessment of Coronary Inflammatory Risk From Noncontrast Cardiac Computed Tomography.
abstract: Importance Individuals with low or minimal coronary artery calcification (CAC) are considered at low cardiovascular risk, but a substantial absolute number of cardiovascular events occur in this population; assessment of coronary inflammation using the fat attenuation index (FAI) score may identify residual inflammatory risk beyond CAC score. Objective To assess whether coronary inflammation measured on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) or noncontrast cardiac CT (NCCT) identifies individuals at high cardiovascular risk independent of CAC burden. Design, setting, and participants In this cohort study, a novel artificial intelligence algorithm for measuring FAI score on NCCT was trained and tested in an independent, multicenter, longitudinal cohort of consecutive individuals undergoing clinically indicated CCTA and NCCT for CAC score between 2010 and 2021, with median (IQR) follow-up of 6.7 (4.6-10.0) years. Data were analyzed from January 2010 to March 2024. Exposure Agatston CAC score and coronary inflammation from both CCTA (CCTA FAI score, established biomarker) and NCCT (NC FAI score, novel biomarker). Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was cardiovascular (CV) mortality; the secondary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), comprising myocardial infarction, new-onset heart failure, or CV death. Results The derivation cohort included 6818 individuals (median [IQR] age, 61 [51-71] years; 3543 female participants [52.0%]), and the external validation clinical outcomes cohort included 19 110 individuals (median [IQR] age, 56.0 [48.0-64.0] years; 9289 female participants [48.6%]). During follow-up, 536 CV deaths and 1727 MACE occurred. FAI scores independently stratified CV mortality risk across CAC score categories, with the strongest associations among individuals with CAC score of 0. Adding CCTA FAI score or NC FAI score to CAC score significantly improved risk discrimination (area under the curve increased from 0.76 to 0.81 and 0.80, respectively; P < .001), reclassification (net reclassification index), and net benefit across all risk thresholds. Among 89 CV deaths in individuals with CAC score of 0 and 138 CV deaths with CAC score of 1 through 99, 44.9% and 44.2% had NC FAI score above the 75th percentile, respectively. Among individuals with CAC score of 0, CV mortality rates increased from 1.4 to 4.0 per 1000 person-years for those with NC FAI score above the 75th percentile, and MACE rates increased from 5.9 to 13.3 per 1000 person-years. Conclusions and relevance Per the results of this cohort study, NC FAI score provides prognostic performance comparable to CCTA FAI score and improves cardiovascular risk prediction and reclassification beyond CAC score. Elevated FAI score, derived from either CCTA or NCCT, should be interpreted as a risk-enhancing factor that may prompt intensification of established, evidence-based preventive measures and may serve as a potential future gatekeeper for the use of targeted anti-inflammatory treatments.

title: Population-Based Evaluation of a Multidimensional Diagnostic Schema for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease.
abstract: Importance A multidimensional chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) diagnostic schema incorporating imaging and clinical features beyond airflow obstruction has been proposed. However, its implications for prevalence, case composition, and prognostic stratification in the general population remain unknown. Objective To compare the population-level classification and prognostic implications of a multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema with those of the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) definition. Design, setting, and participants This population-based cohort study used the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study, conducted at 6 Swedish university hospitals 2013-2018 to compare diagnostic definitions in the full cohort and in a symptom-restricted subgroup approximating routine clinical practice, with mortality follow-up through September 30, 2024. Randomly sampled adults aged 50 to 64 years with complete classification data, including postbronchodilator spirometry and chest computed tomography assessment of emphysema and bronchial wall thickening were included. Exposure Classification according to the multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema and an operationalized GOLD definition. Main outcomes and measures COPD prevalence, case composition, and all-cause mortality. Results A total of 29 281 participants (15011 females [51.3%]; mean [SD] age, 57.5 [4.3] years) were included; 1347 participants (4.6%) met multidimensional COPD criteria. In analyses restricted to 6016 symptomatic individuals, prevalence was similar under the multidimensional and GOLD definitions (909 [15.1%] vs 853 [14.2%]), but case composition differed. Approximately one-third of patients with multidimensional COPD (281 of 909 [30.9%]) did not meet the GOLD criteria. Across the full cohort, 438 individuals (32.5% of multidimensional COPD cases) were asymptomatic and would be unlikely to undergo diagnostic evaluation in routine symptom-driven care. During follow-up, 634 deaths occurred. Among symptomatic participants, adjusted mortality risk was increased in multidimensional-only cases (hazard ratio [HR], 2.58; 95% CI, 1.66-4.01) and those meeting both definitions (HR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.59-3.04), but not in patients with GOLD-only COPD (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.44-2.00). Conclusions and relevance In this population-based cohort study, COPD prevalence was similar with a multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema to that obtained using GOLD criteria, but case composition differed substantially. The multidimensional schema identified increased mortality risk among individuals not captured by GOLD, suggesting improved prognostic stratification, while the identification of many asymptomatic cases highlights an existing detection gap in current symptom-driven care pathways.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Mammography Outcomes by Advanced Breast Cancer Risk.
abstract: Importance Few studies have examined advanced breast cancer rates in women undergoing routine mammography and/or breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Objective To compare screening outcomes of breast MRI vs mammography by advanced breast cancer risk and screening round. Design, setting, and participants This cohort study included women aged 40 to 74 years who had a screening MRI performed with or without a screening film, digital, or digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) mammogram within 12 months (MRI group) or a screening digital or DBT mammogram (mammography-only group) performed at breast imaging facilities participating in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2021, and breast cancers diagnosed between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2022. Data analysis was performed from April 2025 to August 2026. Exposures MRI and mammography; advanced breast cancer risk score calculated using the BCSC advanced cancer risk model and categorized as low (0% to <0.172%), average (0.172% to <0.3797%), intermediate (0.3797% to <0.6582%), or higher (≥0.6582%). Main outcomes and measures Advanced (prognostic stage II or higher) and screen-detected early-stage (prognostic stage I) invasive cancer and false-positive biopsy recommendation rates per 1000 examinations adjusting for registry, examination year, age, race and ethnicity, family history, prior breast biopsy, and breast density. Results A total of 172 865 examinations performed in 105 532 women (median [IQR] age, 52 [46-59] years) were studied. After mammography, the intermediate to high vs low to average risk group had significantly higher advanced cancer (0.6 vs 0.3; difference, 0.4; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6), screen-detected early-stage cancer (2.8 vs 1.8; difference, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.5-1.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (18.1 vs 14.7; difference, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.7-5.2) rates per 1000 examinations. In the MRI group, rates per 1000 examinations of advanced cancer (0.8 vs 1.1; difference, -0.3; 95% CI, -1.3 to 0.7), screen-detected early-stage disease (10.3 vs 11.4; difference, -1.1; 95% CI, -4.9 to 2.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (94.0 vs 93.3; difference, 0.7; 95% CI, -9.9 to 11.3) were not significantly different between intermediate to high and low to average advanced cancer risk groups. Advanced cancer rates were not significantly different for MRI vs mammography between risk groups (difference, 0.6; 95% CI, -0.4 to 1.6). Screen-detected early-stage rates were significantly higher for MRI vs mammography for low to average risk (11.4 vs 1.8; difference, 9.6; 95% CI, 7.3-12.0) and intermediate to high risk (10.3 vs 2.8; difference, 7.5; 95% CI, 4.9-10.1) groups as were false-positive biopsy recommendation rates for low to average risk (93.3 vs 14.7; difference, 78.6; 95% CI, 72.5-84.8) and intermediate to high risk (94.0 vs 18.1; difference, 75.9; 95% CI, 68.3-83.5) groups. Women who underwent subsequent vs first MRIs had significantly lower advanced cancer rates (0.4 vs 2.0; difference, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.3-2.8) and higher advanced cancer risk (median [IQR] BCSC advanced cancer risk score, 0.348 [0.238 to 0.490] vs 0.301 [0.213 to 0.429]; P < .001). Conclusions and relevance In this cohort study, intermediate to high advanced breast cancer risk was associated with higher advanced cancer rates with screening mammography. MRI screening was associated with higher screen-detected early-stage cancer rates compared with mammography but not lower advanced cancer rates, except among women who underwent repeat MRIs. These results suggest that women with elevated advanced cancer risk should discuss MRI screening with their physician.

title: Importance of Angina Pectoris by Coronary Artery Disease Severity.
abstract: Importance Angina pectoris remains a common clinical manifestation, but contemporary population-based data on its long-term prognostic significance are limited. Objective To evaluate the long-term importance of angina pectoris in association with coronary artery disease (CAD) severity determined by coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) in a general population. Design, setting, and participants This population-based cohort study included participants from the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study who had completed the Rose Questionnaire and underwent valid CCTA from November 2013 to October 2018, excluding participants with prior myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure, or coronary revascularization. Follow-up continued through September 2024. Data analyses were conducted between August 2025 and January 2026. Exposures Angina (defined by the Rose Questionnaire) and CAD (categorized as no findings, nonobstructive CAD [<50% stenosis], or obstructive CAD [≥50% stenosis]) according to CCTA findings. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was MI or coronary death. The secondary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as MI, coronary revascularization, heart failure hospitalization, or death from coronary disease or heart failure. Associations were evaluated using Cox regression with sequential multivariable adjustment and stratification by CAD category and presented as hazard ratios (HRs). Results This study included 24 176 individuals (median [IQR] age, 57 [54-61] years; 12 225 female [50.6%]; 1615 with hyperlipidemia [6.8%]; 4374 with hypertension [18.3%]; 703 with diabetes [2.9%]). Angina was present in 720 participants (3.0%). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 7.7 (6.9-8.6) years, 293 primary events occurred. Angina was associated with a higher incidence of MI or coronary death compared with no angina (21 participants [2.9%] vs 272 participants [1.2%]; HR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.60-3.90). Event rates increased across CAD categories, with no evidence of interaction between angina and CAD severity. After multivariable adjustment, angina remained independently associated with the primary outcome (HR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.04-2.63). Similar associations were observed for MACE (adjusted HR, 2.34; 95% CI, 1.73-3.16). Conclusions and relevance In this cohort study of a contemporary general population, angina pectoris was associated with adverse cardiac outcomes, independent of CAD severity assessed by CCTA. These findings suggest that symptom assessment remains relevant in cardiovascular risk stratification because it provided incremental prognostic information that may reflect underlying coronary microvascular dysfunction or vasomotor disorders.

title: Computed Tomography Screening and Small Cell Lung Cancer Stage Shift and Survival.
abstract: Importance Lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) has been shown to identify lung cancers at earlier stages and to significantly reduce lung cancer mortality in prior randomized clinical trials. However, the benefit of LDCT screening for small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive subtype of lung cancer, is unclear. Objective To investigate the characteristics and outcomes of SCLC diagnosed after a lung cancer screening examination using a large database of Medicare beneficiaries. Design, setting, and participants In this retrospective cohort study, Medicare data linked to the Surveillance Epidemiology End Results Program's cancer registry data were analyzed. Patients in the US aged 65 to 78 years who were diagnosed with SCLC from 2015 to 2021 were identified for analysis, with follow-up data through 2022. Patients who underwent 1 or more LDCT lung cancer screening examinations during the 12 months preceding their SCLC diagnosis were included in the screened group. All other patients were included in the unscreened group. Data were analyzed from January to August 2026. Exposure One or more LDCT lung cancer screenings during the 12 months preceding SCLC diagnosis. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcomes were stage at SCLC diagnosis and overall survival after SCLC diagnosis in the screened and unscreened groups. Results A total of 17 099 patients (median [IQR] age, 72.0 [69.0-75.0] years; 8999 [52.6%] female) met study inclusion criteria, of which 949 (5.5%) were included in the screened group and 16 150 (94.5%) were included in the unscreened group. When compared with patients in the unscreened group, patients in the screened group were significantly less likely to be diagnosed with distant disease (419 of 949 [44.2%] vs 11 376 of 16 150 [70.4%]; P < .001). Patients in the screened group also had significantly better overall survival when compared with patients in the unscreened group (3-year overall survival, 28.0% [95% CI, 24.9%-31.2%] vs 10.8% [95% CI, 10.3%-11.3%]; P < .001). Both findings were consistent in propensity score-matched analysis. Conclusions and relevance Results of this cohort study of Medicare beneficiaries diagnosed with SCLC suggest that receipt of lung cancer screening was associated with a shift toward earlier-stage SCLC at diagnosis and improved overall survival.

title: A Preoperative Grading System for Endoscopic Sinus Surgery.
abstract: Importance Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is common, yet one-third of patients do not achieve clinically meaningful improvement after endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS). Existing preoperative measures capture only a portion of the prognostic landscape, and no tool integrates patient-reported phenotype, symptom severity, and objective imaging into a single ordinal index for surgical prognosis. Objective To develop a CRS Severity Index (CRS-SI) that integrates patient-reported symptom phenotypes, characterized across symptom duration categories, with objective imaging measures to estimate the probability of clinically meaningful improvement after ESS. Design, setting, and participants Prospective cohort study with longitudinal data collected from academic tertiary care rhinology clinics between January 2020 and May 2025; follow-up was assessed at 3, 6, and 12 months after surgery. Participants were consecutive patients with CRS aged 16 to 95 years for whom medical management failed and who underwent ESS. Exposures Baseline 22-item Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) measures, symptom phenotype dimensions derived from multiple correspondence analysis, polyp status, Lund-Mackay, and Lund-Kennedy scores. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was clinically meaningful improvement, defined as SNOT-22 improvement of at least 8.9 points from baseline to follow-up. Seven candidate predictors were organized into clinical (baseline SNOT-22, latent symptom phenotype dimensions, polyp status) and imaging (Lund-Mackay, Lund-Kennedy, frontal opacification) arms. CRS-SI was derived using sequential sequestration and conjunctive consolidation. Results Of 488 eligible patients with at least 1 postoperative SNOT-22, 450 with complete clinical and imaging grading data comprised the analytic cohort. Among 450 patients (mean [SD] age, 55.5 [16.3] years; 54.7% [246 of 450] male), 64% achieved clinically meaningful improvement. Of 7 candidate predictors, 6 met bivariate screening criteria (rank-biserial |r|≥0.1 with 95% CI excluding 0). Sequential sequestration selected baseline SNOT-22 severity and a headache and/or chemosensory-dominant symptom phenotype as clinical classifiers, and Lund-Mackay and Lund-Kennedy scores as imaging classifiers. The 4-grade CRS-SI produced a monotonic improvement gradient (grade 1, 81% [95% CI, 72%-88%] to grade 4, 29% [95% CI, 19%-40%]), with a risk difference of 52.5 (95% CI, 39.3-65.7) percentage points between best and worst grades. Discrimination was moderate (C statistic, 0.692; 95% CI, 0.643-0.740) and exceeded imaging grading alone; bootstrap calibration slope, 1.00 (95% CI, 0.77-1.31). Performance was consistent across CRS phenotypes and time points. Conclusions and relevance In this study, a 4-level CRS Severity Index integrating patient-reported symptom profiles with computed tomography and endoscopic imaging stratified improvement after ESS across a 52 percentage-point gradient. If validated externally, the CRS-SI may support preoperative counseling and clinical trial stratification.

title: Diagnosis and Management of Acute Cholangitis: A Review.
abstract: Importance Acute cholangitis (AC) is a potentially fatal biliary tract infection most commonly caused by gallstones. While modern-day treatments with antibiotics and biliary decompression have drastically decreased mortality rates, AC still requires prompt intervention. Observations Diagnosis of AC traditionally relied on the presence of the Charcot triad, which has since proven to incompletely capture the complexity of this condition. Modern-day diagnosis, severity grading, and management guidelines provide a more holistic approach. Tokyo Guidelines (TG) are widely used, though newer guidelines, namely the BILE criteria, have recently emerged. These criteria include demonstration of inflammation, cholestasis, and biliary obstruction. Ultrasound is first-line imaging modality with computed tomography or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography often used for diagnostic dilemmas. Treatment is dependent on severity, though guidelines generally recommend early decompression (most commonly with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography [ERCP]) for moderate to severe cases. The optimal timing of biliary drainage remains unclear, with mixed evidence from observational studies and no universal definition of what constitutes "early" vs "urgent" drainage. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy should be performed during index hospitalization, when possible, with multiple studies demonstrating lower morbidity and mortality rates when compared with interval procedures. The prognosis of AC is favorable if treated swiftly and appropriately; in turn, mortality rates increase with severity and delays in diagnosis. Conclusions and relevance AC can be challenging to diagnose and the precise timing of biliary drainage and cholecystectomy is debated. This comprehensive review reflects the most recent evidence and recommendations on severity grading, resuscitation, and timing of ERCP and cholecystectomy to assist clinicians who manage these complex patients.

title: Diagnostic image quality of shoulder magnetic resonance imaging at 0.55T in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury: Prospective comparison with 1.5T.
abstract: Background Lower‑field 0.55 T MRI scanners with large‑bore design could offer patients more comfortable feeling and flexible position. With the advances in deep‑learning reconstruction and hardware optimization, 0.55T have greatly improved their image quality and cost‑effectiveness for musculoskeletal applications. However, its feasibility for shoulder evaluation remains unstudied. Purpose To evaluate the image quality of shoulder using 0.55T MRI in volunteers and patients with rotator cuff injury with comparison of conventional 1.5T. Methods Fifty participants (25 volunteers, 25 patients) were prospectively enrolled. All participants underwent shoulder MRI both at open 0.55T with contour coils and deep learning (DL) and 1.5T MR without DL. The nonparametric method was utilized to compare image quality scores and quantitative metrics (signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (|CNR|)). Arthroscopy have been conducted in 16 patients. Kappa statistics was used to assess interobserver and interstudy agreement for lesion evaluation. Comfort feeling was also compared. Results The scan time was 11'25″ for 0.55T MRI and 11'42″ for 1.5T MRI. The interobserver analyses showed high consistency (κ = 0.771-1.000, P: 0.008 ∼ < 0.001) among 3 readers. The scores for coronal fat suppressed T2 weighted imaging (fsT2WI) and coronal T1 weighted imaging (T1WI) were significantly higher for 0.55T MRI. Most sequences at 0.55T demonstrated significantly higher SNRs (P:0.04 ∼ < 0.001). Additionally, |CNR| values for lesions were significantly higher in fs proton weighted imaging (PDWI) and fsT2WI at 0.55T. Perfect interstudy agreement between 0.55T and 1.5T was observed between 2 readers (Kappa = 1, P < 0.001) for lesion assessment. Agreement between MRI findings and arthroscopic results was perfect or good. The 0.55T system received higher scores in comfort ratings. Conclusion The 0.55T MRI with DL, showed comparable or better image quality in healthy subjects and patients with rotator cuff injury to 1.5T MRI without DL.

title: Precise anatomical delineation in ultrasound imaging using echo-spectral interactive networks.
abstract: Background Accurate ultrasound (US) segmentation is challenging because speckle noise, low contrast, and ambiguous tissue interfaces often obscure anatomical boundaries. Many conventional CNN- and Transformer-based models operate primarily in the spatial domain and may not explicitly incorporate boundary-related spectral cues. Purpose To develop a spatial-frequency interactive segmentation framework designed to support boundary delineation in US images. Methods We introduce the Echo-Spectral Interactive Transformer (ESI-Former) block, which uses a Spectrum-Directed Self-Attention (SDSA) module to inject differentiable DCT-derived spectral representations into self-attention. We further introduce a Skip-Aware Attention Fusion Module (SAFM) to adaptively fuse encoder skip features with decoder representations. Based on these components, we construct a U-shaped segmentation architecture termed SF-EchoNet. Results SF-EchoNet was evaluated on the TN3K thyroid nodule segmentation dataset and the benign subset of the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset. It achieved run-level mean mIoU scores of 88.01% and 79.58%, with numerically lower run-level mean HD95 values of 41.31 and 47.22, respectively, than the compared methods. Efficiency evaluation showed 12.24M parameters, 9.98 ms latency, and approximately 100 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. Conclusions On the two evaluated public datasets, SF-EchoNet achieved higher run-level mean overlap scores and numerically lower run-level mean HD95 values than the compared methods. Paired analyses supported the overlap differences on both datasets, whereas the magnitude of the mean HD95 difference on the BUSI benign subset remained uncertain. Generalizability to other datasets, acquisition settings, and downstream clinical tasks requires further validation.

Based on these components, we construct a U-shaped segmentation architecture termed SF-EchoNet.

Results

SF-EchoNet was evaluated on the TN3K thyroid nodule segmentation dataset and the benign subset of the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset. It achieved run-level mean mIoU scores of 88.01% and 79.58%, with numerically lower run-level mean HD95 values of 41.31 and 47.22, respectively, than the compared methods. Efficiency evaluation showed 12.24M parameters, 9.98 ms latency, and approximately 100 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.

On the two evaluated public datasets, SF-EchoNet achieved higher run-level mean overlap scores and numerically lower run-level mean HD95 values than the compared methods. Paired analyses supported the overlap differences on both datasets, whereas the magnitude of the mean HD95 difference on the BUSI benign subset remained uncertain. title: Field junction technique in MRI-guided ultra-hypofractionated radiotherapy for a long continuous target volume in prostate cancer: First clinical application, dosimetric and early toxicity outcomes.
abstract: Background MRI-guided radiotherapy (MRIgRT) on a 1.5 T MR-Linac is constrained by a 22 cm maximum field length, limiting long continuous planning target volumes (PTVs). A dual-isocenter field-junction technique has been previously validated in a phantom study. This work presents its first clinical application in hypofractionated prostate radiotherapy. Materials and methods A 79-year-old prostate cancer patient had six contiguous target volumes (PTV, CTV4000, PTVpubis, PGTVpubis, PTVp and PGTVnd), treated over 5 fractions with prescribed doses to the respective target volumes. PTVp was divided into PTVpup and PTVpdn, with a field overlap region between them. Two composite volumes were created: inferior volume (PTV, CTV4000, PTVpubis, PGTVpubis, PTVpdn) and superior volume (PTVpup, PGTVnd), each with its own isocenter. The inferior volume followed the adapt-to-shape (ATS) workflow. During its delivery, the superior volume was first optimized offline on daily MR images using dose feathering approach based on the inferior dose distribution. The optimized plan was then transferred for online adapt-to-position (ATP) adaptation. The inferior and superior volumes were combined offline for dose summation. The ArcCHECK phantom and ArcherQA Monte Carlo method were used for dose verification. Patient-reported outcomes, including FACT-P questionnaires, were collected during the 3-month follow-up. Results Treatment was delivered over 5 alternate-day fractions. ArcCHECK phantom gamma passing rates, using 3%/2 mm with a 10% threshold, were 96.7%, 97.1%, and 96.0% for the inferior, superior and composite reference plans, respectively. Daily ArcherQA showed consistently high passing rates across five fractions: 97.08%-98.43% for the inferior and 98.12%-98.74% for the superior volumes. CTV4000, PTV, PTVpubis and PGTVpub all met prescribed doses. PGTVnd and PTVp had intermittent underdose relative to initial prescriptions, but all fractions met second prescription limits. Organ at risks (OARs) constraints, especially for rectum and bladder, remained within tolerance across all fractions. Total treatment time decreased from 112 min in the first fraction to 80 min in the fifth fraction. FACT-P score declined from 69.17 at baseline to 55.5 at end-of-RT, partially recovering to 57.5 at 2.5 months. No urological or gastrointestinal toxicity was reported during follow-up. Conclusion The proposed two-isocenter field junction technique is clinically feasible for MRIgRT of long continuous prostate cancer PTVs. It provides a practical solution for treating long PTVs on a 1.5 T MR-Linac.

title: Attention Xception U-Net (AXUNet): An explainable combination of CNN and self-attention for reliable glioma segmentation in MRI.
abstract: Background Gliomas are the most common primary malignant brain tumors and exhibit highly heterogeneous morphology and infiltrative growth patterns. Accurate delineation of tumor subregions in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is therefore critical for diagnosis, treatment planning, and longitudinal monitoring, yet manual segmentation remains time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability. Purpose Accurate glioma segmentation in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis, treatment planning, and reproducible tumor delineation. However, for clinical adoption, automated segmentation systems must provide not only high accuracy but also robustness and interpretability. This study aimed to develop an explainable and reliable deep learning framework for glioma segmentation and to evaluate its performance on both internal and external datasets. Method We used the BraTS 2021 training dataset, which contains 1251 multi-institutional pre-operative glioma MRI cases. After comparing multiple sequence combinations, T1ce, T2, and Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) were selected as the final three-channel input. Preprocessing included tumor-oriented slice selection, cropping, Min-Max normalization, and augmentation. We developed AXUNet, a UNet-based architecture that integrates memory-efficient Xception blocks with a self-attention module combining kernel-based pixel attention and dot-product channel attention. Internal ablation analysis and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM)-based visualization were also performed. Results On the BraTS 2021 test partition, AXUNet achieved the highest mean Dice score (93.73), outperforming UNet (93.26), Inception-UNet (90.88), Attention Gate UNet (AG-UNet) (90.38), Attention ResUNet (AResUNet) (92.80), and Xception-UNet (93.24). Region-wise Dice scores were 92.59 for Whole Tumor (WT), 86.81 for Tumor Core (TC), and 84.89 for Enhancing tumor (ET). Although AResUNet achieved a slightly higher ET score (84.92), AXUNet demonstrated the strongest performance in mean Dice, WT, and TC. To further assess generalizability, AXUNet was independently evaluated on 219 previously unseen BraTS 2023 cases through the Synapse platform, achieving Dice scores of 86.29% for WT, 78.53% for TC, and 69.00% for ET. Conclusion AXUNet demonstrates that combining Xception-based encoding with self-attention can improve glioma segmentation while also supporting explainability and external robustness, positioning it as a promising framework for MRI-based glioma segmentation. Its clinical relevance, and the practical value of its interpretability outputs, remain to be established through further, dedicated validation beyond Dice-based benchmarking.

title: A virtual physicist framework integrating dose prediction and large language models for automated treatment planning.
abstract: Background Automated radiotherapy treatment planning has benefited from data-driven approaches; however, achieving consistently high plan quality across patients remains challenging. Dose prediction models provide patient-specific priors but lack adaptive optimization, whereas large language models (LLMs) offer strong reasoning capabilities but raise concerns regarding stability and safety in clinical use. Purpose To develop and validate a fully automated VMAT treatment planning framework integrating dose prediction and LLM-driven dynamic optimization, termed the Virtual physicist (VP), and to evaluate its dosimetric performance, plan complexity, and consistency relative to manual and other automated planning strategies. Methods A total of 70 cervical cancer patients previously treated with VMAT were retrospectively collected. The dataset was divided into 50 cases for training, 10 for validation, and 10 for testing. The input data consisted of patients' planning CT images with contoured planning target volumes (PTVs) and organs at risk (OARs). The outputs included predicted three-dimensional dose distributions (upper-, middle-, and lower-dose bands) and automatically generated VMAT treatment plans with corresponding dosimetric and plan complexity metrics. The VP framework was implemented in the MOZI treatment planning system via a Python scripting interface. A dose-band prediction model was used to initialize patient-specific optimization constraints. During optimization, an LLM iteratively adjusted objectives and weights based on real-time dosimetric feedback, subject to a rule-based safety engine enforcing clinical and physical constraints. Plans generated using dose prediction only (DP-only), LLM only (LLM-only), and combined dose prediction with LLM (DP + LLM) were compared with clinically delivered manual plans. Results The DP + LLM strategy significantly improved sparing of the bladder and bilateral femoral heads compared with all three other strategies and significantly reduced rectal doses relative to the DP-only and manual plans (P < 0.05), while maintaining PTV Dmean, HI, CI, and GI comparable to those of the manual plans (P > 0.05). For dual-layer MLC plan complexity, DP + LLM produced a more balanced modulation pattern than manual planning, with lower distal-layer complexity-significant for d-C/A and d-MCS but not d-BA-and higher proximal-layer complexity across all three metrics. Compared with DP-only and LLM-only plans, DP + LLM showed a consistent trend toward greater complexity in most metrics, with significant differences in several metrics. In addition, the automated strategies generally showed smaller standard deviations in complexity metrics, indicating improved planning consistency. Conclusion Integrating dose prediction with LLM-driven dynamic optimization enables a robust and fully automated planning workflow, improving OAR sparing and planning consistency without compromising target dose quality, and demonstrates strong potential for clinically applicable intelligent radiotherapy planning.

title: Assessment of simulated respiratory gating based on external-to-internal motion prediction using a hybrid, adaptive deep-learning network.
abstract: Purpose To assess the accuracy, safety, and efficiency of respiratory-gated radiotherapy (RGRT) based on internal respiratory waveforms predicted by a hybrid long short-term memory (LSTM) deep-learning network, which adapts to breathing irregularities through the application of time-domain cross-correlation (TCC) to check and correct any residual phase/time shift in the LSTM predictions. Methods The adaptive LSTM-TCC model was built in two steps: (1) subject-specific LSTM models were trained to predict internal diaphragm motion from external bellows motion using each of 10 subjects' concurrent waveforms (≥20 Hz, 3-10 min) acquired from four-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (4DMRI) protocol scans and (2) near real-time TCC was applied to the LSTM predictions to check and correct any residual phase/time shifts to safeguard against new breathing irregularities beyond the training data in the mid-term (3-10 min) and long-term (20-30 min) datasets. The testing datasets comprised both the mid-term and long-term concurrent motion waveforms, and the external-to-internal motion predictions and gating quality assessments for each subject were evaluated and validated with the actual internal motion as the ground truth. The hybrid LSTM-TCC models were compared with LSTM, TCC, and native external-to-internal correlation models. The temporal gating accuracy (beam-off and beam-on) and beam-gating quality (missing-target rate: %harm, and beam-on efficiency: %effic) of the hybrid LSTM-TCC model were evaluated and compared with LSTM, TCC, and native predictions. Results The hybrid LSTM-TCC models produced the highest long-term sustained correlations (C > 0.8, within 30 min), yielding the lowest %harm = 5 ± 6% and the highest %effic = 67 ± 15%, compared with the LSTM (%harm = 8 ± 8%, %effic = 65 ± 16%), the TCC (%harm = 29 ± 31%, %effic = 43 ± 19%), and the native (%harm = 37 ± 23%, %effic = 38 ± 14%). The hybrid LSTM-TCC models produced a high, sustained performance (C = 0.9 ± 0.1) without remodeling, regardless of new breathing irregularities, and the average temporal error of the predicted gating windows was ∆t < 0.3 s. Conclusion This study assesses the simulated respiratory-gating qualities of four methods, demonstrating that the hybrid LSTM-TCC approach outperforms the native waveforms, the TCC method, and the LSTM models, yielding the highest correlation, gating accuracy, and %effic, but the least %harm. The hybrid LSTM-TCC model can safeguard LSTM predictions and gating accuracy against major breathing irregularities, demonstrating a strong potential for future clinical applications.
