title: Interdisciplinary regenerative management of a radicular cyst associated with a cemental tear and external inflammatory resorption: A case report.
abstract: Background Cemental tears are rare clinical entities where a portion of the cementum detaches from the root surface, often leading to localized periodontal or periapical destruction. They are frequently misdiagnosed as vertical root fractures or primary endodontic lesions. This case reports on the successful interdisciplinary management of a radicular cyst associated with a cemental tear and external inflammatory resorption (EIR). Methods A 63-year-old female presented with a sinus tract and radiographic evidence of apical and lateral radiolucency involving teeth #9 and #10. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) identified a cemental tear and an unobturated lateral canal on the necrotic tooth #9, and EIR with a periapical/periodontal abscess on tooth #10, which had been previously root canal treated. Tooth #9 received initial nonsurgical root canal therapy, while tooth #10 received nonsurgical retreatment; both were followed by a combined surgical approach involving apicoectomy of both teeth, removal of the cemental tear, and periodontal regeneration using enamel matrix derivative, platelet-rich fibrin, and bone allograft. Results Histopathologic analysis confirmed a radicular cyst. The cemental tear and lateral canal on tooth #9 were confirmed intraoperatively under the surgical microscope. At 2-week, 4-week (suture removal), 2-month, and 6-month follow-up, including CBCT re-evaluation, the patient exhibited favorable soft-tissue healing and resolution of clinical symptoms. Conclusion A coordinated endodontic‒periodontal microsurgical approach utilizing advanced regenerative biomaterials achieved favorable short-term clinical and radiographic healing of a complex lesion involving a cemental tear, lateral canal, EIR, and radicular cyst, allowing preservation of both teeth. Longer follow-up is needed to confirm the durability of these results. Key points Cemental tears and lateral canals are easily overlooked on two-dimensional radiographs and can mimic vertical root fractures or routine endodontic‒periodontal lesions; cone-beam computed tomography combined with direct microsurgical inspection improves diagnostic accuracy. A coordinated, single-stage endodontic‒periodontal surgical approach-combining apicoectomy, cemental tear removal, and regenerative therapy (enamel matrix derivative, platelet-rich fibrin, and bone allograft)-can achieve favorable short-term healing and avoid extraction, even in teeth with combined periapical and periodontal involvement. Histopathologic confirmation remains essential for definitive diagnosis of radicular cysts and for verifying suspected cemental tear fragments; longer-term follow-up is needed to confirm the durability of regenerative outcomes. Plain language summary A small piece of the outer covering of a tooth root, called cementum, can sometimes separate from the tooth. This is called a cemental tear, and it is easy to miss because it can look like a cracked tooth or a common gum infection on X-rays. In this case, a 63-year-old woman had ongoing infection near her upper front teeth. Detailed three-dimensional imaging (a type of dental computed tomography scan) revealed a cemental tear on one tooth and slow, ongoing damage to the root surface of a neighboring tooth, along with a fluid-filled cyst at the site. A dental specialist team performed root canal treatment, then surgically removed the damaged piece of tooth root and used tissue-healing materials, including a gel derived from tooth-forming proteins and a concentrate made from the patient's own blood, to help the bone and gum tissue heal. Six months later, healing looked favorable both clinically and on imaging, and the patient's teeth were saved rather than removed. This case shows how combining advanced imaging with a coordinated effort between root canal and gum specialists can help save teeth that might otherwise need extraction, though longer follow-up is needed to confirm the healing lasts.

Detailed three-dimensional imaging (a type of dental computed tomography scan) revealed a cemental tear on one tooth and slow, ongoing damage to the root surface of a neighboring tooth, along with a fluid-filled cyst at the site. A dental specialist team performed root canal treatment, then surgically removed the damaged piece of tooth root and used tissue-healing materials, including a gel derived from tooth-forming proteins and a concentrate made from the patient's own blood, to help the bone and gum tissue heal. Six months later, healing looked favorable both clinically and on imaging, and the patient's teeth were saved rather than removed. This case shows how combining advanced imaging with a coordinated effort between root canal and gum specialists can help save teeth that might otherwise need extraction, though longer follow-up is needed to confirm the healing lasts.

title: Guided bone regeneration using CAD-CAM zirconia barriers: A case series with digital evaluation of bone changes.
abstract: Background CAD/CAM zirconia barriers represent an advanced option for guided bone regeneration (GBR) in three-dimensional defects, integrating mechanical stability, biocompatibility, and digital precision. The objectives of this case series were to evaluate, clinically, histologically, and three-dimensionally, the use of customized zirconia barriers designed using CAD/CAM technology in GBR procedures. Methods and results Three patients with severe maxillary bone atrophy were included and treated with GBR using customized zirconia barriers. Digital planning was performed based on cone beam computed tomography and intraoral scanning, followed by CAD/CAM design and fabrication of the barriers. The defects were regenerated using a mixture of autogenous bone and xenograft. After the healing period, implants were placed using guided surgery, and bone biopsies were obtained for histological analysis. Bone gains were evaluated through linear and volumetric digital analysis based on three-dimensional model superimposition. All surgeries were completed without complications, allowing implant placement in all cases without the need for additional augmentation procedures. Mean horizontal bone gains of 6.17 mm at the crestal level and mean vertical gains of 2.62 mm were recorded, with maximum values of up to 5.11 mm. Volumetric analysis revealed bone gains of 797.158 mm 3 (case 1), 459.718 mm 3 (case 2), and 1416.870 mm 3 (case 3). Histological analysis demonstrated vital, well-vascularized newly formed bone undergoing active remodeling, with no evidence of inflammation. Conclusions Customized zirconia barriers demonstrated favorable clinical and histological outcomes in GBR. The digital workflow, combined with three-dimensional analysis, allowed a precise and reproducible evaluation of bone changes. Key points This case series presents a comprehensive clinical protocol for guided bone regeneration using customized zirconia barriers, based on prosthetically driven planning, individualized barrier design, graft stability, and meticulous peri-implant soft tissue management, including histological analysis of the regenerated tissue. The incorporation of a standardized digital protocol for linear and volumetric analysis enabled an objective, reproducible, and precise evaluation of dimensional changes in the alveolar ridge. Plain language summary Significant bone loss in the upper jaw can prevent dental implants from being placed in the correct position. In these situations, rebuilding the lost bone is necessary to achieve a stable long-term outcome. This case series describes the use of customized zirconia barriers designed to fit each bone defect and support bone regeneration. After the healing period, all treated defects showed sufficient bone gain to allow implant placement according to the original prosthetic treatment plan. Histological analysis confirmed the formation of new bone, while a standardized digital measurement protocol provided an objective and reproducible assessment of the bone changes achieved after treatment. These findings suggest that customized zirconia barriers may represent a promising alternative for the management of complex bone defects, although studies involving larger numbers of patients are needed to confirm these results.

title: Sequential Coronary Obstruction After Native TAVI: Immediate Acute Occlusion and Very Late Stent Compression by Aortic Wall Hematoma.
abstract: Coronary obstruction is a rare but catastrophic complication of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) associated with high mortality. While acute and delayed presentations have distinct pathophysiological mechanisms, their occurrence in the same patient is exceedingly rare. We present a unique case of a 91-year-old female who developed acute left main coronary artery (LMCA) obstruction immediately following native TAVI using a balloon-expandable valve, which was successfully treated with bail-out percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Three months later (> 60 days, classified as "Very Late" coronary obstruction), she presented with severe angina and heart failure. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) revealed extrinsic compression of the previously implanted coronary stent caused by a localized aortic wall hematoma. A repeat PCI with a stent-in-stent technique restored coronary flow, leading to complete clinical recovery. This case expands the known mechanical spectrum of very late coronary obstruction according to recent classification frameworks and highlights the vital role of intravascular imaging and multimodality assessment in diagnosis and management.

title: Transcatheter Thrombus Removal With the Penumbra Indigo Lightning System in Children With Congenital Heart Disease.
abstract: Thromboembolic complications in children with congenital heart disease (CHD) carry significant morbidity and mortality, particularly in patients with single ventricle physiology. Current management strategies, including systemic anticoagulation, thrombolytics, and surgical thrombectomy, each carry substantial risks in this population. Transcatheter aspiration thrombectomy represents an emerging alternative. We retrospectively reviewed all pediatric patients with CHD at our institution who underwent transcatheter aspiration thrombectomy using the Penumbra Indigo Lightning System between January 2024 and February 2025. Patient demographics, cardiac diagnosis, thrombus location, procedural details, and clinical outcomes were recorded. Five patients (age 5 months to 9 years; weight 6.3-25.9 kg) with diverse CHD diagnoses underwent six thrombectomy procedures. Thrombus locations included the Fontan circuit, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, and internal jugular veins. Technical success with angiographic restoration of antegrade flow and no residual gradient across the segment of interest, was achieved in all cases (100%). Blood loss ranged from 6 to 23 mL/kg; all patients required packed red blood cell transfusion. No significant intraprocedural hemodynamic instability occurred. Three patients were discharged home with confirmed vessel patency on follow-up imaging (echocardiography and/or vascular ultrasound at 4-6 months post intervention). Two patients, both on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support prior to the procedure, subsequently died from causes unrelated to the thrombectomy intervention. In this limited case series, the Penumbra Indigo Lightning System demonstrated feasibility for transcatheter thrombus removal in pediatric patients across a spectrum of CHD. Given the limited number of available catheter systems in this population, this approach may be considered as a first-line or adjunct therapy in select patients when conventional medical management is insufficient or contraindicated. Further prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection, procedural techniques, and post-procedural management.

title: Urgent True-Lumen Recovery Using Tip-Detection Antegrade Dissection and Re-Entry for Ongoing Myocardial Ischemia Caused by Progressive Subintimal Space Expansion.
abstract: Progressive subintimal space expansion during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is a serious complication that may compress the true lumen, impair coronary flow, and cause ongoing myocardial ischemia. Tip-detection antegrade dissection and re-entry (TD-ADR) is an intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-guided re-entry technique developed for chronic total occlusion (CTO) intervention; however, its role as an emergency bailout strategy during non-CTO PCI remains unclear. An 84-year-old woman underwent elective PCI for a severely stenotic, tortuous left anterior descending artery lesion. Repeated guidewire attempts resulted in progressive subintimal space expansion with true-lumen compression, coronary flow deterioration, chest pain, and ischemic ST-segment elevation. As further parallel-wire attempts were considered unlikely to restore distal true-lumen access and risked further enlarging the subintimal space, IVUS-guided TD-ADR was adopted as an emergency bailout strategy. With the AnteOwl WR IVUS catheter and a Finecross GT-supported Conquest Pro 12 ST penetration wire positioned in parallel within the subintimal space, repeated transducer sweeps enabled real-time identification of the wire tip, its direction, and the target true lumen. Re-entry was achieved with a single puncture, followed by advancement of the microcatheter into the true lumen and exchange to a soft workhorse wire. Cutting-balloon fenestration then decompressed the subintimal space, after which drug-eluting stents were implanted. Final angiography demonstrated TIMI 3 flow and a satisfactory angiographic result. Peak creatine kinase was 560 U/L, follow-up echocardiography showed no new regional wall-motion abnormalities, and the patient was discharged without complications. This case suggests that TD-ADR may represent a valuable emergency bailout strategy for urgent true-lumen recovery in selected non-CTO PCI cases complicated by progressive flow-limiting subintimal space expansion. Early recognition of failed conventional wiring and timely conversion to TD-ADR may facilitate myocardial salvage.

title: Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension Complicated by Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome: A Case Series of Two Patients.
abstract: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a rare but potentially life-threatening neurological complication associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. This report presents two cases of pregnancy-induced hypertension complicated by PRES, both clinically characterized by headache and visual disturbances, with characteristic neuroimaging findings. The clinical manifestations, laboratory findings, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics of two patients are described. Following prompt multidisciplinary consultation and immediate interventions, including strict blood pressure control, seizure prophylaxis, infection prevention, and appropriate obstetric management, both patients achieved favorable clinical outcomes. No significant neurological abnormalities were observed at the 42-day postpartum follow-up. In patients with severe pregnancy-induced hypertension, PRES warrants recognition as a potential complication; management should prioritize rigorous blood pressure control, seizure prophylaxis, alleviation of pregnancy-related physiological stress, and timely neuroimaging to guide treatment, with strategies balancing maternal and fetal safety-early recognition and intervention underpinned by standardized protocols and multidisciplinary collaboration being critical to improving prognosis and reducing complications.

title: Acute Hematemesis Leading to the Incidental Diagnosis of Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma in an Adolescent: First Case Report From Pakistan.
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is exceptionally rare in children and adolescents and typically presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss. Its occurrence without conventional risk factors may pose a diagnostic challenge. A 16-year-old boy presented with acute hematemesis and no history of dysphagia, odynophagia, or recognized esophageal cancer risk factors. He was undernourished, with a BMI of 17 kg/m 2 and progressive unquantified weight loss. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a deep proximal esophageal ulcer, distal esophageal ulcers, a Mallory-Weiss tear, and gastritis. The latter lesions offered potential explanations for the bleeding, but the atypical proximal ulcer raised suspicion for malignancy, prompting biopsy. Histopathology confirmed moderately differentiated ESCC with high-grade dysplasia. Contrast-enhanced CT showed localized upper thoracic esophageal wall thickening without regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastases, and the disease was staged as T2N0M0. The patient completed three cycles of neoadjuvant carboplatin-paclitaxel-based chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy. A repeat endoscopy showed a circumferential raw mucosal area with a superficial erosion in the distal esophagus, while the upper and middle thirds of the esophagus appeared normal; however, esophagectomy was recommended as part of the planned definitive management. This case highlights the incidental discovery of ESCC during evaluation of acute hematemesis in an adolescent without conventional risk factors. Hematemesis with low BMI or unexplained weight loss should prompt careful evaluation for underlying esophageal pathology, even when an apparent benign bleeding source is identified. Early biopsy, appropriate staging, and multidisciplinary management are essential for timely diagnosis and treatment.

title: Menstrual-Associated (Catamenial) Pneumothorax With Hepatic Herniation Through an Advanced Porous Diaphragm.
abstract: Catamenial pneumothorax pathophysiology is heterogeneous; visceral herniation without histologic endometriosis is rare. A 38-year-old with recurrent catamenial pneumothorax underwent robotic repair revealing 8 cm diaphragmatic fenestrations with transdiaphragmatic hepatic herniation; histopathology confirmed no endometrial tissue. We propose a three-tiered classification to guide clinical reasoning when histopathology is inconclusive.

title: Rapidly Growing Fetal Cervical Mass: Prenatal Diagnostic Insights and Perinatal Management Considerations-A Case Report.
abstract: Fetal cervical masses are rare anomalies associated with significant perinatal morbidity due to potential airway obstruction. The main differential diagnoses are cervical teratoma and lymphatic malformation, two entities whose prognosis and management differ substantially. We report the case of a 38 year-old gravida 3 para 0 woman in whom a fetal anterior neck mass was identified at 17 weeks' gestation. Serial ultrasound demonstrated rapid growth with progressive solid-cystic components, calcifications, hypervascularity and polyhydramnios, whereas the fetal MRI report initially favored a cystic lymphatic malformation. Multidisciplinary evaluation favored a cervical teratoma; the EXIT strategy was ultimately ruled out primarily because predicted lethal pulmonary hypoplasia at a very early gestational age made survival unlikely even with a secured airway, and secondarily because massive tumor extension made airway access unlikely to succeed. Compassionate termination of pregnancy was offered; the parents opted for a planned cesarean delivery with neonatal comfort care, but spontaneous preterm labor occurred at 26 + 1 weeks and a stillborn male infant was delivered by emergency cesarean section. Postmortem examination confirmed a predominantly mature congenital cervical teratoma. This case illustrates the diagnostic value of serial imaging, the complementarity of ultrasound and MRI, and the centrality of multidisciplinary decision-making.

title: Right Ventricular Dysfunction and Ventriculo-Arterial Uncoupling in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Phenotype-Specific Review of Mechanisms, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for nearly half of all global heart failure cases. Historically viewed as a left-centric diastolic disorder, emerging evidence identifies right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and impaired ventriculo-arterial (RV-PA) coupling as central drivers of exercise intolerance, functional decline, and adverse clinical outcomes. Objectives This review synthesizes current evidence on the pathophysiological mechanisms, advanced diagnostic modalities, prognostic implications, and phenotype-specific therapies for RV dysfunction in HFpEF, advocating for a transition to systematic biventricular evaluation. Methods A structured, PRISMA-informed search of PubMed and Scopus (2015-2024) identified 74 eligible studies evaluating RV structure, function, and hemodynamics in HFpEF cohorts. Results RV dysfunction is prevalent in 19% to 33% of HFpEF patients and independently predicts all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations. Key pathophysiological drivers include post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, impaired RV lusitropy, systemic inflammation, and inter-ventricular dependence. Non-invasive markers notably speckle-tracking echocardiography, 4D-flow cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), and the TAPSE/PASP ratio enable early identification of subclinical RV-PA uncoupling. While traditional heart failure therapies show limited efficacy, emerging options including SGLT2 inhibitors, interatrial shunt devices, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and targeted pulmonary vasodilators demonstrate potential to preserve RV strain and restore hemodynamics across distinct clinical phenotypes. Conclusions RV dysfunction is a major prognostic marker in HFpEF. Routine inclusion of RV-PA coupling indices in diagnostic and risk-stratification algorithms is essential to guide precision-based, phenotype-guided management and improve clinical trajectories.

Background

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for nearly half of all global heart failure cases. Historically viewed as a left-centric diastolic disorder, emerging evidence identifies right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and impaired ventriculo-arterial (RV-PA) coupling as central drivers of exercise intolerance, functional decline, and adverse clinical outcomes.

Objectives

This review synthesizes current evidence on the pathophysiological mechanisms, advanced diagnostic modalities, prognostic implications, and phenotype-specific therapies for RV dysfunction in HFpEF, advocating for a transition to systematic biventricular evaluation.

Methods

A structured, PRISMA-informed search of PubMed and Scopus (2015-2024) identified 74 eligible studies evaluating RV structure, function, and hemodynamics in HFpEF cohorts.

Results

RV dysfunction is prevalent in 19% to 33% of HFpEF patients and independently predicts all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations. Key pathophysiological drivers include post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, impaired RV lusitropy, systemic inflammation, and inter-ventricular dependence. Non-invasive markers notably speckle-tracking echocardiography, 4D-flow cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), and the TAPSE/PASP ratio enable early identification of subclinical RV-PA uncoupling. While traditional heart failure therapies show limited efficacy, emerging options including SGLT2 inhibitors, interatrial shunt devices, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and targeted pulmonary vasodilators demonstrate potential to preserve RV strain and restore hemodynamics across distinct clinical phenotypes.

Conclusions

RV dysfunction is a major prognostic marker in HFpEF. Routine inclusion of RV-PA coupling indices in diagnostic and risk-stratification algorithms is essential to guide precision-based, phenotype-guided management and improve clinical trajectories.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Stenotic Pressure-Drop Estimation From 4D Flow MRI: Validation Against In Vitro Measurements.
abstract: Estimating pressure drops non-invasively from 4D Flow MRI velocity data remains challenging: analytical and direct inverse estimators are efficient but sensitive to resolution and noise, whereas Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) requires uncertain boundary conditions and substantial preprocessing. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a complementary framework by enforcing the Navier-Stokes equations on measured velocity fields, but their robustness under MRI-like data degradation requires validation. We performed an experimental stenosis benchmark to validate a PINN framework for pressure estimation from internal velocity measurements, without prescribed inlet or outlet boundary conditions. Using a 3D-printed stenotic phantom under steady and pulsatile flow conditions, the approach was evaluated against: (1) high-fidelity CFD, (2) synthetic 4D Flow MRI at 1- to 3-mm resolution, and (3) pressure transducer measurements. Against noise-free CFD, the PINN achieved high fidelity (pressure Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) <3% ). Synthetic MRI tests showed that accuracy was strongly governed by spatial resolution. At 1 mm, pressure-drop errors remained <5% for moderate flows but reached ≈30% in high-velocity cases. At 3 mm, degraded flow features led to ≈50% underestimation in steady cases and reduced flow-rate consistency in pulsatile conditions. At adequate resolution, PINN-derived pressure drops agreed with transducer measurements. This study provides a controlled benchmark of PINN-based pressure reconstruction from 4D Flow MRI-like data, not a direct clinical validation. PINNs can recover pressure fields without prescribed boundary conditions, but exhibit resolution-related limitations similar to lightweight pressure estimators such as PPE, STE, and vWERP. Thus, they should be viewed as complementary tools rather than replacements for established estimators. Clinical translation will require resolved imaging and dedicated developments, such as MRI-aware losses or sub-voxel modeling, to mitigate data degradation.

title: Sarcomatoid Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma With Well-Differentiated Squamous Cell Carcinoma Misdiagnosed as Liver Abscess: A Case Report.
abstract: Background Sarcomatoid intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (sICC) is a rare and highly aggressive variant of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Due to overlapping clinical and imaging features, it is frequently misdiagnosed as benign hepatic lesions, such as bacterial liver abscesses. Case Herein, we report a case of a 59-year-old male patient who presented with fever and right upper abdominal pain. Laboratory tests revealed markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage was performed, and Hafnia alvei was cultured from the purulent fluid. Combined with abscess-like imaging manifestations and tumor necrosis with possible secondary infection, the case was preoperatively misdiagnosed as a bacterial liver abscess. The patient underwent a laparoscopic partial hepatectomy. Intraoperative frozen-section pathology suggested a hepatic malignant tumor, and the final postoperative diagnosis confirmed sICC with well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Despite aggressive surgical intervention, the patient's condition rapidly deteriorated with imaging suggestive of tumor progression, and he died of multiple organ failure approximately 10 weeks after the initial surgery. Conclusion This case underscores the diagnostic pitfall of sICC presenting as a liver abscess. Puncture or drainage of such necrotic masses should be performed with caution due to the risk of tumor cell dissemination. Early recognition, timely biopsy, and aggressive radical resection are crucial for improving the prognosis of this rare entity.

title: Carcinoma In Situ Skip Lesions of the Uterine Corpus in Cervical Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Impact on Target Setting in Radiotherapy.
abstract: Background In definitive radiotherapy for FIGO Stage I-III cervical cancer, external beam radiotherapy and/or brachytherapy are used-alone or in combination with concurrent chemotherapy depending on stage-with target delineation largely guided by clinically apparent disease. However, discontinuous carcinoma in situ (CIS) "skip lesions" within the uterine corpus are well described in cervical adenocarcinoma, whereas their presence in cervical squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) has not been systematically evaluated. Aims This study aimed to investigate the presence or absence of CIS skip lesions in the uterine corpus of patients with cervical SCC. Methods and results This retrospective study included all patients who underwent total or radical hysterectomy for cervical SCC at Yamagata University Hospital between January 2013 and April 2020. Patients who underwent prior radiotherapy or preoperative chemotherapy, or had non-squamous histological components, were excluded. Fifty patients were enrolled. Pathological examination of serially sectioned uterine specimens was conducted to identify skip lesions, defined as discontinuous CIS lesions in the uterine corpus, as confirmed by a pathologist and a radiation oncologist. Pathological evaluation showed that 29 patients (58%) had FIGO Stage I disease, 6 patients (12%) had FIGO Stage II disease, and 15 patients (30%) were classified as FIGO Stage IIIC1. Preoperative imaging studies did not identify any skip lesions in the uterine corpus. However, one patient (2%; Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence intervals: 0.05%-10.5%) presented with a histologically confirmed CIS skip lesion located in the uterine corpus, approximately 2 cm cranial to the primary tumor margin, that was undetectable on imaging. The primary tumor after biopsy measured 3 mm and was diagnosed as non-keratinizing SCC without > 1/3 stromal invasion. Lymphovascular space invasion, parametrial invasion, and corpus invasion were not observed. Conclusion Although rare, CIS skip lesions in the uterine corpus can occur in patients with cervical SCC.

title: White Matter Geometric Disorganization Links Subcortical Degeneration to Motor Impairment in Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3.
abstract: Background Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3) is the most common hereditary ataxia caused by CAG repeat expansion in the ATXN3 gene. However, the structural mechanisms linking genetic burden, neurodegeneration, and motor impairment remain poorly understood. Methods This multicenter cross-sectional study included 105 genetically confirmed patients with SCA3 and 133 healthy controls. Diffusion MRI and structural MRI were acquired using harmonized protocols and harmonized across sites using ComBat. Director field analysis (DFA) was used to quantify WM geometric organization (splay, bend, and twist). Voxel-wise, region-of-interest, correlation, and mediation analyses were performed to examine associations among WM geometry, subcortical atrophy, CAG repeat length, and motor impairment measured by the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA). Results SCA3 patients exhibited widespread increases in splay and bend together with reductions in twist across cerebellar peduncles, projection, commissural, and association fibers. Geometric abnormalities were substantially more extensive than alterations detected by conventional diffusion metrics. Significant atrophy was observed predominantly in the cerebellar white matter, brainstem, putamen, globus pallidus, thalamus, and caudate. Longer CAG repeat expansions were associated with greater geometric disruption within motor-related pathways. Furthermore, geometric abnormalities within the external capsule and superior cerebellar peduncle partially mediated the association between basal ganglia atrophy and motor impairment. Conclusion White matter geometric alterations may represent a potential imaging phenotype linking genetic burden, subcortical neurodegeneration, and motor disability in SCA3. These findings provide new insights into the network mechanisms underlying disease progression and highlight WM geometric metrics as potential imaging biomarkers for SCA3.

title: Advancing Clinical Trials and Precision Medicine in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Using Machine Learning-Based Trajectory Modeling and MRI Radiomics.
abstract: Given heterogeneous progression of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), accurately characterizing individual disease trajectories is critical for effective clinical trials and therapeutic development. In this study, we applied machine learning (ML) approaches leveraging disease progression models and baseline magnetic resonance (MR)-derived radiomic features to quantify individual-level DMD progression trajectories and support quantitative characterization of disease progression. Radiomic features were extracted from segmented soleus (SOL) and vastus lateralis (VL) fat-fraction maps, generating 810 features per individual, with additional functional and demographic measures incorporated as covariates following feature selection. Multiple ML regressors were trained and validated to estimate MR-spectroscopy fat-fraction trajectory descriptive parameters: DPT 50 (age at half-maximal increase), DP max (extent), γ (rate), S 0 (extrapolated measure at age 0). Key radiomic features were identified through feature importance analyses, followed by downstream analyses, including unsupervised clustering. The tree-based XGBoost regression model demonstrated best future longitudinal fat-fraction trajectories (SOL: mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.04, R 2 = 0.94; VL: MAE = 0.06, R 2 = 0.95). Subsequent downstream analyses highlighted potential key biomarkers clinically associated with DMD progression. Clustering analysis revealed clinically meaningful slow- and fast-progression subgroups with interpretable decision criteria (SOL: DPT 50 = 12.21 vs. 14.83; γ = 8.07 vs. 7.54, VL: 10.37 vs. 14.21; γ = 7.72 vs. 7.09) that can inform clinical trial designs and therapeutic effects within homogenous groups. Individual-level feature importance interpretation further shows the possibility of tailoring personalized intervention strategies. These findings highlight the potential of ML-based trajectory modeling approaches leveraging baseline MRI radiomics for advancing AI-assisted clinical trial development and precision medicine, charting a new direction for MRI-guided disease modeling in neuromuscular disorders.

title: Automated Detection of Positioning Errors in Bitewing Radiographs Using Deep Learning.
abstract: Objectives Bitewing radiographs (BWs) are essential diagnostic tools in dentistry, but are often affected by positioning errors, compromising their diagnostic value and increasing retake rates. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a deep learning-based automated system for detecting and classifying BW type (premolar/molar), side (right/left), and common positioning errors in a controlled mannequin-based setting. Methods A total of 403 BWs were collected from dental student assessments acquired from dental radiology mannequins. BWs were consensus-labeled by dentomaxillofacial radiology experts for type, side, and the most common positioning errors. A balanced data set supported training and validation. Convolutional neural network architectures, including ResNet and DenseNet variants, were trained from scratch and evaluated as independent classification tasks using stratified fivefold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the curve, reported as mean ± standard deviation across folds. A confusion matrix was generated for multi-class cone-cutting error (CCE) severity classification. Results The system achieved accuracies of 95.8% for BW type classification, 99.0% for side classification, 96.3% for CCE detection, and 93.4% for interproximal overlap detection. Multi-class CCE classification achieved an accuracy of 79.3%, with reliable identification of "critical" and "minimal" errors. Detection of incorrect receptor placement achieved an accuracy of 73.2%. Conclusions The CNN-based system showed strong performance for bitewing type, side, binary cone-cutting error, and interproximal overlap classification in mannequin-acquired radiographs. Performance was more limited for multi-class cone-cutting severity and incorrect receptor placement. These findings support the potential use of deep learning for radiographic quality assessment in education and quality-control workflows. A validation study using patient-acquired bitewing radiographs from clinical settings is required before clinical deployment.

title: Gender Variations in Alveolar Process Dimensions and Maxillary Anterior Tooth Inclination: A CBCT-Based Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Objectives Due to the unique anatomy of the maxillary anterior esthetic zone, placing an implant immediately post-tooth extraction can be challenging. The success of immediate implant placement largely relies on the shape of the alveolar bone and the angle of the extracted tooth. This cross-sectional study is designed to evaluate the dimensions of the alveolar bone in the maxillary anterior region using cone beam computed tomography (CBCT). Methods and material Maxillary anterior region scans from 60 individuals (30 males, 30 females) were assessed using CBCT. Statistical analysis accounted for the clustering of teeth within individual participants. They were subjected to CBCT scans, examined for alveolar process thickness (APT), facial bone thickness (FBT), facial bone thickness at the apex (FBTA) in mm and Tooth inclination in degrees in the maxillary anterior teeth including central incisors (CI), lateral incisors (LI) and canines. Results The mean values for APT and FBTA for all teeth groups were found to be greater in males, while there was no gender difference between the FBT values. FBTA values were significantly greater for CI and LI in males. A strong inverse relationship was observed in males for tooth inclination with FBTA for all teeth, while in females, it was observed only for tooth inclination with FBTA for CI (p ˂ 0.05). Conclusions This study demonstrates distinct gender and tooth-specific variations in APT, FBTA, and tooth inclination across the maxillary anterior region. Among all evaluated parameters, FBTA was identified as the sole alveolar bone feature independently associated with tooth inclination after adjusting for covariates and within-subject clustering. Consequently, these findings offer vital anatomical and radiographic insights to aid treatment planning and enhance clinical outcomes in anterior maxillary procedures. Trial registration CTRI number: CTRI/2022/06/055457; Registered with Clinical Trial Registry India on 04/07/2022.

title: Triphasic waves in leptomeningeal metastases and cycling alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep.
abstract: Background Triphasic waves (TWs), now termed generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology, may be mistaken for nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE), particularly in critically ill patients. Changes in vigilance over time can help distinguish encephalopathic patterns from ictal activity. Case presentation A 69-year-old woman with breast cancer and leptomeningeal metastases developed progressive mutism and impaired consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed atypical cells and markedly elevated protein, while brain MRI demonstrated bilateral sulcal hyperintensities, most prominent in the posterior regions. An EEG performed 1 week after bevacizumab and paclitaxel were discontinued showed only mild background slowing without epileptiform discharges. A repeat EEG 1 week later showed nearly continuous TWs. The discharges disappeared during spontaneous sleep and recurred periodically, consistent with a cyclic alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep (CAPE). In the absence of significant metabolic and toxic derangements, these features favored an encephalopathic rather than ictal pattern. Given the advanced disease and poor prognosis, care remained supportive and palliative. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of interpreting TWs within their clinical context and in relation to the state of vigilance. Their disappearance at sleep onset, with periodic recurrence during sleep producing a CAPE, supports an encephalopathic rather than ictal interpretation, helping to avoid misdiagnosis of NCSE and unnecessary administration of antiseizure medications.

title: Direct cortical electrical stimulation-induced seizures: Are they reliable? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: We aimed to assess the frequency, clinical relevance, and prognostic value of stimulation-induced seizures (SIS) during intracranial EEG recording (iEEG), and to compare high-frequency (HF) and low-frequency (LF) stimulation protocols. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting SIS during preoperative iEEG. Pooled proportions of SIS and habitual seizures were estimated using random-effects models. Differences between HF and LF stimulation were assessed using odds ratios. Study-level meta-regression was conducted to evaluate associations between SIS rates, habitual seizure proportions, and postoperative favorable seizure outcome (Engel Ia). Twenty-five studies were included. SIS occurred more frequently with HF than LF stimulation (56.1% vs. 35.8%; OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.50-2.23; p < 0.001), with substantial between-study heterogeneity. Among patients with SIS, LF stimulation was associated with a higher proportion of habitual seizures compared to HF (81.8% vs. 72.9%), although this difference was not statistically significant. A higher proportion of habitual electro-clinical seizures among SIS correlated with increased rates of favorable seizure outcomes with LF stimulation (p = 0.004) but not with HF stimulation (p = 0,912). Finally, MRI-visible lesions and the mesio-temporal seizure-onset zone were associated with higher SIS rates (p < 0.01). In conclusion, HF stimulation increases the likelihood of inducing SIS, but SIS frequency was not associated with a higher proportion of favorable seizure outcomes. Instead, the clinical relevance of SIS depends on their similarity to habitual seizures. These findings suggest that SIS may reflect underlying network excitability, and that their diagnostic value lies in their semiological and EEG concordance rather than occurrence of stimulated seizures alone. Overall, these results emphasize the importance of stimulation-induced habitual electro-clinical seizures for postsurgical outcome prognostication.

title: Repetitive clustered low-voltage fast activity on intracranial electroencephalogram in mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia and epilepsy: A candidate electroencephalographic biomarker study.
abstract: Objective Mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia and epilepsy (MOGHE) is a recently recognized cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy. It is often magnetic resonance imaging-negative or radiologically resembles focal cortical dysplasias, which makes recognition difficult and limits presurgical counseling. We aimed to identify an intracranial electroencephalographic (iEEG) biomarker that distinguishes MOGHE from other developmental brain lesions encountered in epilepsy surgery. Methods We analyzed long-term stereo-EEG and subdural recordings in a retrospective multicenter test cohort (18 MOGHE, 20 non-MOGHE) to identify an iEEG pattern distinguishing MOGHE from other developmental brain lesions. We then evaluated its diagnostic performance by blinded visual assessment in an independent single-center validation cohort (11 MOGHE, 11 non-MOGHE). Firth-penalized multivariable logistic regression tested whether MOGHE histology independently predicted the presence of this pattern after adjustment for spasms, frontal localization, age at seizure onset, and age at implantation. Finally, within MOGHE, we assessed whether resection of the territory exhibiting this pattern was associated with postsurgical seizure freedom. Results We identified highly stereotyped clusters of very brief low-voltage fast activity (LVFA), recurring in statuslike episodes lasting several minutes and sometimes lacking clear clinical symptoms. LVFA clusters occurred in 16 of 18 MOGHE and in no non-MOGHE patients in the test cohort. In the validation cohort, visual identification of LVFA clusters correctly classified 10 of 11 MOGHE and 10 of 11 non-MOGHE cases (overall agreement = 90.9%, 95% Wilson confidence interval = 72.2%-97.5%). MOGHE histology was the dominant independent predictor of LVFA clusters. Within MOGHE, resection of LVFA cluster territory was associated with postsurgical seizure freedom (Mann-Whitney U-test, p = .0021). Significance Because LVFA clusters can be recognized visually on routine iEEG without specialized software, they may provide a clinically applicable candidate biomarker for presurgical identification of MOGHE and support surgical planning and outcome prediction. Prospective studies should validate their diagnostic and prognostic utility.

title: Integrating uncertainty and practice variability for epilepsy prognostication after intracranial EEG: A meta-analysis.
abstract: Objective Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) practices and diagnostic testing vary among institutions, limiting standardization and optimization of surgical outcomes. This study estimates resection rates and surgical outcome effect sizes after iEEG and develops individual patient-level data (IPD) models using the missing-indicator method to approximate real-world clinical uncertainties and practice variability in iEEG and surgical decision-making. Methods Databases were queried for studies reporting ≥12-month outcomes after epilepsy surgery in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) who underwent iEEG. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled outcome proportions. IPD analysis was performed using multivariable generalized linear regression and logistic regression models with cross-validation and calibration assessment. Missing values for key predictors were retained as a "not specified" category to evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty in common clinical data on outcome prediction. Results Primary outcomes were seizure freedom (Engel class IA or International League Against Epilepsy [ILAE] 1) and favorable seizure outcomes (Engel I or ILAE 1-2). Of 4975 studies identified, 115 met the inclusion criteria. The pooled frequency of patients undergoing resection after iEEG was 67% (95% confidence interval [CI] 60%-74%), 52% achieved seizure freedom (95% CI 48%-56%), and 58% achieved a favorable outcome (95% CI 54%-62%). IPD analysis included 1305 patients from 29 studies and identified a lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; odds ratio [OR] 1.94, CI 1.48-2.55, p < .0001) and a cortical malformation (OR 1.47, CI 1.08-2.00, p = .01) as independent predictors of a favorable outcome, whereas iEEG implantation strategy (bilateral implantation OR .61, 95% CI .42-.89, p = .01) was an independent predictor of a less favorable outcome. Significance About two-thirds of patients undergoing iEEG proceeded to resection, and about half achieved seizure freedom. Multivariable models incorporating clinical uncertainty and practice variability were well calibrated. However, modest discrimination suggests that routinely available clinical variables alone have limited ability to predict individual surgical outcomes. More standardized and granular clinical and practice-related data may improve individualized prognostication after iEEG.

title: Validation of drug-resistant epilepsy identification algorithms in US Veterans across diverse care settings.
abstract: Objective Early recognition of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is critical for timely referral to comprehensive epilepsy centers (CECs). Our prior pilot study in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) demonstrated the feasibility of an algorithm-based approach to identify DRE within selected CECs. In this study, we validated and refined these algorithms in a broader, national cohort, including CEC and non-CEC care, to optimize algorithms for different care settings. Methods We conducted a multicenter, retrospective study of randomly sampled veterans with epilepsy on ≥2 antiseizure medications (ASMs) from 1999 to 2024. Chart review by 26 epilepsy providers rated DRE status. Ninety-six candidate algorithms using combinations of six criteria-number of ASMs, treatment duration, dose thresholds, pregabalin exclusion, intractable International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes, and electroencephalography (EEG)/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) utilization-were evaluated. Performance for DRE classification was evaluated among all veterans, and separately for CEC or non-CEC care. Results Among 970 veterans on ≥2 lifetime ASMs, 518 (53.4%) were rated as DRE, 363 (37.4%) as non-DRE, and 89 (9.2%) as undetermined. Veterans with DRE were younger (mean age = 68.9 vs. 72.0 years) and more frequently had at least one intractable ICD code (46.1% vs. 18.2%), EEG (77.8% vs. 66.7%), or MRI (78.0% vs. 65.8%) compared with non-DRE (all p-values <.001). This algorithm was also highly effective among veterans who received CEC (AUC = .756) or only non-CEC care (AUC = .678). Significance This national validation study confirms that medication-based algorithms can identify DRE within VHA administrative data across care settings (CECs and non-CECs). This supports the implementation of a standardized DRE definition for quality improvement, surveillance, and referral optimization within the VHA.

title: Scalp high-frequency oscillations differentiate neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with and without electroencephalographically confirmed seizures.
abstract: Objective Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is a leading cause of neonatal seizures, but seizure detection is challenging when continuous electroencephalography (EEG) is unavailable and neonates undergo only a single routine EEG. Biomarkers derived from routine EEG may aid identification of neonates with seizures. We investigated whether scalp high-frequency oscillation (HFO) rates derived from the first eligible routine EEG (1) differentiate neonates with HIE with and without seizures; and (2) contribute to seizure classification alongside established clinical, neurophysiological, and imaging biomarkers. Methods We retrospectively analyzed routine scalp EEG recordings from 33 term neonates with HIE (17 with seizures, 16 without), obtained at a mean postnatal age of 4 ± 3 days. The mean analyzed EEG duration was 38 ± 14 min in neonates with seizures and 36 ± 20 min in those without. HFO rates in sleep segments were quantified using a validated automated detector. Results Scalp HFO rates were significantly higher in neonates with seizures than in those without (.12 ± .11 vs. .03 ± .02 HFOs/min/channel, adjusted p = .02). An HFO rate threshold of .07 HFOs/min/channel optimally discriminated neonates who had seizures from those who did not (area under the curve [AUC] = .81). HFO rates did not differ significantly according to HIE severity, therapeutic hypothermia, antiseizure medication response, EEG background activity, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities. Multivariable models incorporating HFO rate, EEG background activity, and MRI findings showed discrimination (AUC = .92, 95% confidence interval [CI] = .69-1.00 for logistic regression; AUC = 1.00, 95% CI = .75-1.00 for random forest), with HFO rate as the strongest contributor to seizure classification. Significance These findings support scalp HFO rate as a potential electrophysiological biomarker of seizure occurrence in neonatal HIE, complementary to EEG background assessment and MRI findings. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether HFOs can predict subsequent seizures.

title: Brain Stiffness Correlation Networks in Healthy Older Adults Using Magnetic Resonance Elastography.
abstract: Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) quantifies tissue stiffness, a measure of microstructural integrity. While gray matter structural correlation networks are well established, the large-scale topological organization of stiffness correlation networks is not fully characterized. This study introduces the biomechanical covariance network framework, in which stiffness correlation networks reflect inter-individual covariation in regional stiffness across participants after adjusting for age, sex, regional gray matter volume, total intracranial volume, and scanner. We tested whether these networks exhibit small-world topology and how they differ from volume correlation networks. MRE-derived stiffness and MRI-derived gray matter volume maps were analyzed from 98 cognitively unimpaired older adults, and correlation networks of 112 gray matter regions were constructed using the Mayo Clinic Adult Lifespan Template (MCALT) ADIR-122 parcellation. The normalized clustering coefficient ( γ ), normalized path length, and small-world index ( σ ) were calculated against degree-preserving null networks across network densities. The stiffness correlation networks exhibited small-world architecture, with high local clustering and short path lengths ( σ = 2.44 at 5% density and above 1 at all densities examined, 5%-51%). Stiffness and volume correlation networks showed partial correspondence (r = 0.306, p < 0.0001) but were not redundant, with the stiffness networks showing stronger local clustering ( γ = 3.01 versus 2.43 at 5% density). These findings establish the biomechanical covariance network framework in cognitively unimpaired older adults and suggest that biomechanical correlations may offer information complementary to volumetric measures. The framework provides a reference for future studies of how these networks change with age, disease, and cognitive decline.

title: Intraoperative Management of Fibular Free Flap With Chronic DVT: Case and Technique.
abstract: Background Chronic post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) involving the peroneal venae comitantes is an uncommon but potentially flap-threatening finding during fibular free flap reconstruction that may not be detected on routine preoperative computed tomography angiography. We describe the successful management of extensive chronic PTS encountered unexpectedly during fibular free flap reconstruction for advanced oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma. Methods Following unsuccessful mechanical thrombectomy, arterial inflow was established before venous reconstruction to identify the dominant functional venous outflow pathway, followed by selective venous anastomosis. Results Early postoperative venous congestion was successfully managed with revision and a second venous anastomosis. The flap remained viable with excellent functional and oncologic outcomes at 1 year. Conclusion This case demonstrates that chronic PTS should not necessarily preclude fibular free flap reconstruction and presents a practical intraoperative and postoperative strategy for managing this challenging and previously underreported scenario.

title: Outcomes Following Extreme Elective Nodal De-Escalation in HNSCC Treated With Curative Intent: A Community Program Experience.
abstract: Purpose/objective(s) To evaluate elective nodal recurrence rates in HNSCC patients treated with extreme dose de-escalation to 30 or 40 Gy followed by a sequential boost to gross disease or high-risk sites. Materials/methods Between May 2017 and May 2025, patients diagnosed with SCC of the oropharynx, larynx, or hypopharynx were treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy or surgery followed by adjuvant (chemo)radiotherapy. Elective nodal volumes (ENV) defined as any uninvolved adjacent, distant ipsilateral or contralateral anatomic nodal level were treated to either 30 or 40 Gy, followed by a sequential boost to the PTVp/PTVn+ or high-risk surgical bed (PTVp+ PTVn+). A subset of 6 patients received 24-36 Gy (1.5-1.8 Gy BID) based on the Mayo-DART regimen. Assignment to 40 Gy versus 30 Gy reflected the radiation oncologist preference based on emerging trial evidence. All cases were reviewed prospectively in a head and neck multidisciplinary conference, and treatment planning required diagnostic FDG PET-CT fused to the planning CT. Concurrent systemic therapy was administered in 99% of patients. The primary endpoint was regional failure rate within the de-escalated ENV. Secondary endpoints included 1- and 2-year locoregional control (LRC), progression-free survival (PFS), distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), and failure patterns. Results The analysis included 102 patients of whom the majority 81.4% received definitive chemoradiotherapy, 17.6% underwent surgery with adjuvant chemoradiotherapy, and 1% received surgery with adjuvant radiation alone. The elective nodal volume was treated to 40 Gy at 2 Gy per fraction in 81 patients and to 30 Gy at 2 Gy per fraction in 15 patients; the remaining 6 adjuvant patients received 24-36 Gy at 1.5-1.8 Gy twice daily per the Mayo-DART regimen. With a median follow-up of 26.4 months, no elective nodal failures were observed in either dose cohort. The 1- and 2-year LRC rates were 93.5%. The 1- and 2-year progression-free survival (PFS) rates were 88.6% and 87.3%, respectively, while distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) rates were 95.0% and 95.0%, respectively. In total, 13 recurrences were recorded comprising 7 locoregional and 6 distant failures. Conclusion This represents the largest report demonstrating the efficacy of extreme dose de-escalation to ENV's for HNSCC within an NCI designated community cancer program. Reduced doses to the ENV ranging from 40 Gy to as low as 30 Gy were associated with exceptionally low failure rates regardless of treatment approach, stage, or HPV, and validate similar findings previously reported from larger academic centers. Importantly, 99% of patients received concurrent systemic therapy, and these results should not be extrapolated to radiotherapy alone.

title: Primary Mediastinal B-Cell Lymphoma in Clinical Practice: A Case-Based Approach to Unresolved Diagnostic and Therapeutic Dilemmas.
abstract: Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) is a rare and biologically distinct subtype of aggressive B-cell lymphoma that predominantly affects young adults. Despite substantial therapeutic advances, several aspects of its management remain controversial, including frontline treatment selection, the role of radiotherapy, PET-based response assessment, and the optimal sequencing of immunotherapies in relapsed disease. Drawing on prospective and retrospective studies, cooperative group data, expert consensus and our own real-world experience, we present a practical case-based approach across the disease course, built around four clinical cases followed to their resolution and covering diagnosis, frontline treatment, PET-guided response assessment, pregnancy-associated disease, adolescents and young adults, relapsed or refractory disease, and long-term follow-up. We focus on decision-making where evidence remains limited, including the integration of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), CAR-T cell therapy, radiotherapy and transplantation, and the emerging role of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and radiomics. Management increasingly relies on individualized, multidisciplinary decision-making that integrates disease biology, functional imaging and patient characteristics to maximize cure while minimizing long-term toxicity. In our practice this translates into dose-intensified frontline chemoimmunotherapy rather than R-CHOP21, omission of radiotherapy after a complete metabolic response and, where these treatments are accessible, a second-line strategy built on checkpoint inhibitors and anti-CD19 CAR-T cells, with early referral for cellular therapy in refractory or early relapse.

title: Mycetoma: A Narrative Review of Its Clinical and Epidemiological Spectrum With a Focus on Iran.
abstract: Background and aims Mycetoma is a chronic, neglected tropical disease affecting the skin and subcutaneous tissues, capable of extending to deeper structures. It exists in two forms: eumycetoma (fungal) and actinomycetoma (bacterial). This review aims to examine the epidemiology, causative organisms, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis, and management of mycetoma, with a specific focus on the situation in Iran. It also seeks to summarize pathogen-directed therapies and evaluate the consistency of published Iranian case data. Methods This is a narrative review of the literature concerning mycetoma, synthesizing global data and published Iranian case series. The review analyzes information on disease classification, causative pathogens, including Actinomadura madurae and Nocardia species, clinical presentation, diagnostic methods, and treatment outcomes. Results Globally, the relative frequency of actinomycetoma and eumycetoma varies by region. In Iran, mycetoma is reported sporadically, with actinomycetoma predominating, although its reported proportion varies considerably among Iranian series (approximately 54%-85%). The disease most commonly affects the feet of adult men in rural agricultural communities. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and grain examination via microscopy, histopathology, and culture. Treatment is pathogen-directed: actinomycetoma typically responds to prolonged antimicrobial therapy (e.g., co-trimoxazole and amikacin), while eumycetoma often requires prolonged antifungal therapy (e.g., itraconazole) and surgery, with less successful outcomes due to poor drug penetration. Conclusion Greater clinical awareness, earlier diagnosis, and appropriate pathogen-directed treatment are critical to prevent disease progression, disability, and amputation in mycetoma patients. Preventive measures remain limited, primarily focusing on reducing exposure to contaminated soil. The review highlights the need for more consistent data reporting in Iran to better understand the disease burden and improve management strategies.

title: Impact of the pink October campaign on breast cancer screening in the Alpes-Maritimes region (France): A regional perspective.
abstract: Objective Our objective was to describe monthly variations in breast cancer screening activity during the Pink October campaign and assess whether the observed increase extended beyond the campaign period in the Alpes-Maritimes region of France. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study of aggregated monthly mammogram counts from January 2022 to December 2024. Data on organized screening (DO) were available for all 3 years, whereas data for individual screening (DP) were available only for 2024. Monthly screening activity during October and November was compared with activity during the remaining months using the statistical methods described below. Results Organized screening activity peaked in October in each study year, with reported increases of 31% in 2022, 27% in 2023, and 48% in 2024 relative to the respective annual monthly means. The October-November comparison yielded P-values of 0.001 in 2022, 0.049 in 2023, and 0.054 in 2024. The 2024 result did not reach the conventional threshold for statistical significance. Individual screening showed a smaller October increase in 2024 (+10% relative to its annual monthly mean), and the October-November comparison was not statistically significant (P = 0.178). These findings describe temporal variations in screening activity and do not establish a causal effect of the campaign. Conclusion Mammography activity, particularly organized screening, increased during the Pink October period in the Alpes-Maritimes region. However, the aggregated data cannot establish whether this increase represented additional screening or a redistribution of examinations across the calendar year. Further multicenter studies using longer time series and individual-level data are needed to assess the campaign's effect on screening participation.

title: Sex-Specific Myostatin-Grey Matter Volume Associations in Ageing Adults: Implications for the Muscle-Brain Axis.
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is increasingly recognized as a risk factor for cognitive decline, suggesting bidirectional muscle-brain crosstalk mediated by myokines. Myostatin, a negative regulator of muscle growth, may influence brain health through systemic signalling, yet human neuroimaging evidence remains lacking. Moreover, men and women exhibit distinct patterns of muscle ageing and cognitive decline, but sex-specific effects of myostatin on brain structure have not been investigated. This study examined associations between serum myostatin and regional brain grey matter volume (GMV) in ageing adults, with emphasis on sexual dimorphism. Methods We analysed 482 community-dwelling participants (235 males, 247 females; mean age 67.2 ± 8.5 years, range of 50-88) from the I-Lan Longitudinal Aging Study. Serum myostatin levels, muscle mass and grip strength were assessed. High-resolution brain MRI was processed using voxel-based morphometry to examine associations between myostatin and regional GMV. Sex-stratified analyses were performed, adjusting for age, muscle metrics and total intracranial volume, with multiple comparison correction (cluster-level FWE p < 0.05). Results Men demonstrated 17.8% higher serum myostatin than women (5227.5 ± 2413.2 vs. 4438.4 ± 1934.1 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and were older (68.4 ± 9.2 vs. 66.0 ± 7.5 years, p = 0.002). Myostatin correlated positively with muscle mass in both sexes (men: r = 0.209, p = 0.001; women: r = 0.181, p = 0.004) but showed no association with grip strength (p > 0.95). Notably, height-adjusted muscle mass correlated with grip strength in men (r = 0.204, p = 0.002) but not women (r = 0.075, p = 0.240). Neuroimaging revealed complete sexual dimorphism with zero overlapping brain regions. In men, higher myostatin associated with larger GMV in left postcentral gyrus but smaller GMV in right cerebellum VIIIb. In women, higher myostatin associated exclusively with smaller GMV across three regions: left inferior temporal gyrus, right frontal pole and right postcentral gyrus. Sensitivity analyses using the ratio of myostatin to relative appendicular skeletal muscle mass (RASM) reproduced the primary associations and revealed additional negative associations in the left cerebellum Crus I in men and in the left temporal pole and left middle temporal gyrus in women. Conclusions Myostatin demonstrated pronounced sex-specific associations with brain structure, with complete sexual dimorphism. Women exhibited exclusively negative myostatin-GMV relationships across cognitive and sensorimotor regions, whereas men showed mixed patterns. These findings provide the first human neuroimaging evidence for sexual dimorphism in the muscle-brain axis. Given that sarcopenia confers two-to threefold greater cognitive impairment risk in women, elevated myostatin may represent a sex-specific biomarker linking muscle wasting to neurodegeneration.

title: Value of Intratumoral and Peritumoral Ultrasound Radiomics Nomogram for Differential Diagnosis of C-TIRADS 4 Thyroid Nodules.
abstract: Objective The Chinese Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (C-TIRADS) 4 thyroid nodules (TNs) have intricate sonographic features that potentially lead to overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis. This study aimed to improve the precision of differentiating C-TIRADS 4 TNs using radiomic nomograms that include both intratumoral and peritumoral features. Methods A total of 337 patients with C-TIRADS 4 thyroid nodules confirmed by pathology or FNAB were retrospectively enrolled and randomly divided into a training cohort (n = 269) and a validation cohort (n = 68) at a ratio of 8:2. Radiomics features were extracted from intratumoral and peritumoral (1-3 mm) regions on B-mode ultrasound images. Feature stability was assessed using intraclass and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Key features were selected through a sequential process involving the Mann-Whitney U test, recursive feature elimination (RFE), and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, followed by calculation of the radiomics score (Rad-score). Independent predictors were identified by univariate and multivariate logistic regression. Three models were constructed: a clinical and ultrasound model (Model 1), a radiomics model (Model 2), and a combined nomogram integrating both (Model 3). Model performance and clinical utility were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results Multivariate analysis showed that age, margin, echogenic foci, and the intratumoral and peritumoral 1 mm Rad-score were independent predictors for the benign or malignant nature of C-TIRADS 4 nodules (p < 0.05). The combined nomogram (Model 3) achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.852 (95% CI: 0.804-0.892) in the training cohort, significantly higher than that of Model 1 (AUC = 0.737) and Model 2 (AUC = 0.784) (p < 0.05). In the validation cohort, Model 3 yielded an AUC of 0.916 (95% CI: 0.851-0.980), outperforming Model 1 (AUC = 0.766) and Model 2 (AUC = 0.807) (both p < 0.05). The calibration curve of the nomogram showed good agreement with the ideal curve (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p > 0.05), and DCA indicated that it provided the greatest clinical net benefit. Conclusion The nomogram integrating clinical characteristics, ultrasound characteristics, and intratumoral and peritumoral 1 mm Rad-score can distinguish benign from malignant C-TIRADS 4 TNs, with superior diagnostic performance compared to single-modality models. It may serve as a non-invasive and reliable tool to reduce unnecessary FNAB rates.

title: Epicardial Fat Thickness in Fetal Growth Restriction: Impact on Neonatal Outcomes and Predictive Value.
abstract: Purpose Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a condition associated with heightened risks of perinatal morbidity and mortality. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) has been identified as a potential marker for metabolic changes in fetuses, but its role in FGR remains underexplored. This study aimed to assess fetal epicardial fat thickness (EFT) in the third trimester and its correlation with FGR diagnosis and fetal measurements. Method A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted at a Perinatology Clinic involving 82 pregnant women, including 43 with FGR and 39 controls. FGR diagnosis was based on Delphi criteria. EFT measurements were performed using echocardiography techniques, and statistical analyses were conducted to assess correlations and predictive values. Fetal EFT was measured using ultrasound, and interobserver reliability was assessed using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). Results In the FGR group, EFT was significantly lower than in controls (p < 0.001). A significant moderate positive correlation was observed between EFT and fetal abdominal circumference (r = 0.363, p = 0.017). ROC analysis identified an EFT cutoff value of ≤ 1.41 mm for discriminating FGR, with 60.5% sensitivity and 92.3% specificity (AUC = 0.802, p < 0.001). In addition, EFT showed significant discriminatory ability for composite adverse neonatal outcomes (AUC = 0.727, p = 0.001). Conclusion This study highlights the potential clinical significance of fetal EFT thickness in FGR diagnosis and neonatal outcome prediction. EFT measurements offer valuable insights into fetal metabolic status and may aid in early identification of high-risk pregnancies. Further research is warranted to validate these findings and integrate EFT assessments into routine prenatal care for improved perinatal management strategies.

title: Thymidine Kinase 2 Deficiency in the Era of Approved Therapy: From Diagnosis to Evidence Across the Disease Spectrum.
abstract: Thymidine kinase 2 deficiency (TK2d) is an ultra-rare autosomal recessive mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the nuclear TK2 gene. Loss of TK2 activity disrupts intramitochondrial deoxynucleotide pools, impairing mtDNA replication and resulting in a spectrum of quantitative (mtDNA depletion) and qualitative (multiple deletions) alterations whose severity is a key determinant of prognosis. Clinically, TK2d presents as a continuous phenotypic spectrum, from rapidly progressive infantile disease to adult-onset forms, predominantly manifesting as progressive myopathy with early bulbar and respiratory involvement, the principal drivers of morbidity and mortality, with overall severity inversely correlated with age at onset. Central nervous system involvement may occur in severe early-onset cases, whilst extramuscular manifestations are otherwise limited, with sensorineural hearing loss and subclinical axonal sensory neuropathy described across the spectrum. Circulating biomarkers, particularly GDF-15, support diagnosis, correlate with disease severity and show dynamic changes with treatment; serum creatinine, muscle MRI fat fraction and forced vital capacity further contribute to prognostic stratification. Oral supplementation with doxecitine and doxribtimine, recently approved by the FDA (2025) and EMA (2026) for patients with symptom onset ≤ 12 years, represents the first disease-modifying therapy for TK2d, demonstrating marked survival benefit, stabilisation of disease progression and partial recovery of motor function. Evidence in adult patients remains limited and largely retrospective, underscoring the need for dedicated prospective studies with outcome measures sensitive to slowly progressive phenotypes.

title: MRI Microscopic Fractional Anisotropy Differences in Genetic Frontotemporal Degeneration.
abstract: Background In genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), cortical and subcortical brain volume differences have been detected using volumetric MRI decades before symptoms appear. Microscopic fractional anisotropy (μFA) is a diffusion MRI metric that is sensitive to diffusion anisotropy regardless of relative fiber orientations within a voxel and is more accurate than conventional DTI metrics for detecting age-related microstructural changes in healthy individuals and differences in some neurological diseases. Purpose To compare μFA, mean diffusivity (MD), and volume between genetic frontotemporal degeneration (FTD) variant carriers and non-carriers in the insula, frontal pole, and medial orbitofrontal cortex. Study type Cross-sectional cohort study. Population Carriers of FTD variants in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT (n = 12; age = 56.7 ± 8.12 years; 50% female) and familial non-variant carriers (n = 8; age = 59.5 ± 10.3 years; 62.5% female). Field strength/sequence 3T; Magnetization prepared rapid acquisition with gradient echoes (MPRAGE) sequence (anatomical imaging) and a diffusion echo-planar imaging sequence with modified diffusion gradients for spherical tensor encoding (μFA measurement). Assessment MPRAGE images underwent cortical and subcortical segmentation to obtain regions of interest. MD and μFA maps were derived from diffusion MRI data. μFA, MD, and volumes were compared between FTD variant carriers (n = 5 symptomatic, and n = 7 asymptomatic) and familial non-carriers. Statistical tests Linear models with heteroscedasticity-consistent confidence intervals were computed to analyze between-group differences in outcomes while controlling for age (alpha = 0.05). Results FTD variant carriers exhibited significantly lower insula μFA than non-carriers (η 2 p = 0.22). Post hoc contrasts showed significantly reduced insula μFA in symptomatic carriers compared to non-carriers (d = 1.57). Mean μFA in asymptomatic carriers (mean ± standard error (SE): 0.454 ± 0.010) was not significantly different to that in non-carriers (mean ± SE: 0.471 ± 0.009, p = 0.465), nor in symptomatic carriers (mean ± SE: 0.430 ± 0.012, p = 0.290). Data conclusion μFA is reduced in the insula, a region vulnerable to early atrophy in FTD, reflecting microstructural changes in genetic FTD with greater effect sizes than MD and volume. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy Stage 2.

title: Fetal Liver Volume and Morphology in Growth-Restricted Fetuses and Their Association With Neonatal Morbidity: An MRI Study.
abstract: Background Fetal growth restriction (FGR) may induce redistribution of the fetal circulation to preserve perfusion of vital organs. Reduced hepatic delivery of oxygen- and nutrient-rich blood may cause volumetric and morphological remodeling. Purpose To quantify fetal liver volume and morphology in FGR and assess associations with adverse neonatal outcomes. Study type Single-center, prospective and retrospective. Population Ninety-two singleton pregnancies: 36 FGR cases (prospective) and 56 appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) controls (retrospective). Field strength/sequence 3-T, True Fast Imaging with Steady-State Free Precession (TrueFISP) for fetal liver and body imaging, and TrueFISP or Half-Fourier Acquisition Single-shot Turbo Spin-Echo for brain imaging. Assessment The fetal liver, body, and brain were segmented using deep learning tools. Liver volume, liver-to-body and brain-to-liver volume ratios, and 12 liver PyRadiomics shape features were assessed. Neonates were followed for composite adverse neonatal outcomes (CANO) until discharge. Statistical tests Linear regression assessed associations with gestational age in AGA fetuses. Linear mixed-effects models compared groups, adjusting for gestational age and fetal sex. Univariable logistic regression assessed associations with CANO. Benjamini-Hochberg correction controlled the false discovery rate at 0.05. Results FGR fetuses had significantly lower liver volume than AGA fetuses (74.95 ± 1.76 vs. 114.89 ± 2.18 cm 3 ), lower liver-to-body ratio (0.053 ± 0.001 vs. 0.057 ± 0.001), and higher brain-to-liver ratio (2.637 ± 0.085 vs. 1.978 ± 0.047). FGR fetuses demonstrated significantly less elongated liver geometry, (10.7% higher PyRadiomics elongation values) and had a significantly higher surface-to-volume ratio (11.9%). CANO occurred in 30/92 neonates (27 FGR, 3 AGA). Higher brain-to-liver ratio (OR = 4.12, 95% CI: 1.93-8.77), PyRadiomics elongation values (less elongated geometry; OR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.26-3.30), PyRadiomics flatness values (less flattened geometry; OR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.07-2.65), and surface-to-volume ratio (OR = 3.26, 95% CI: 1.80-5.90) were significantly associated with CANO. Data conclusion FGR was associated with reduced fetal liver size and altered geometry, which were associated with neonatal morbidity. Evidence level 2. Technical efficacy 2.
