title: Deep learning pulmonary vessel segmentation for contrast-enhanced and non-contrast CT images.
abstract: Background Accurate and comprehensive segmentation of pulmonary vasculature is essential for diagnosing various pulmonary diseases and lung surgical planning. Purpose To develop a deep learning model for pulmonary vessels segmentation based on both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) data, and to evaluate its performance on a clinical dataset. Methods In this retrospective study, we collected 427 cases of chest CT data from different countries and manufacturers, including 213 CTPA cases and 214 NCCT cases. And we designed a CTPA and NCCT ground truth (GT) generation method producing high-accuracy vessel annotation dataset. Then we developed a 3D U-Net based deep learning method with the Vessel Lumen Structure Optimization Module (VLSOM). We numerically evaluated model using metrics including Centerline Recall (Cl-Recall), Centerline DICE (Cl-DICE), Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) and 95% Hausdorff Distance (HD95) focusing on the integrity of vascular structures. Finally, the model performance was visually assessed in an independent external dataset. Results In the numerical evaluation on the internal test dataset with 57 cases, our model achieved Cl-DICE, Cl-Recall and HD95 values of 0.909 (95% CI [0.904, 0.914]), 0.883 (95% CI [0.873, 0.891]) and 1.861 mm (95% CI [1.674 mm, 2.073 mm]) which is superior to the state of the art (SOTA) baseline model nnU-Net v2 of 0.860 (95% CI [0.852, 0.867]), 0.772 (95% CI [0.760, 0.783])and 2.458 mm (95% CI [2.219 mm, 2.708 mm]) (all p < 0.001). In the clinical visual assessments on the 90 sets of external datasets, the average score for accuracy and robustness, branch abundance, computer-aided detection and vascular continuity 4.52 (95% CI [4.42, 4.62]), 4.82 (95% CI [4.76, 4.90]), 4.58 (95% CI [4.46, 4.69]), and 4.85 (95% CI [4.77, 4.92]) respectively with a full score of 5. Conclusions The proposed pulmonary vessel segmentation algorithm performed well in preserving the connectivity and integrity of the vascular structure on both CTPA and NCCT data with various diseases. Critical relevance statement A vessel centerline topology-enhanced deep segmentation model enables accurate and automatic pulmonary vessel segmentation in both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) images.

title: Characterization of local linearity in deep learning CT denoising networks.
abstract: Background Deep learning algorithms for image processing have been proposed for a wide range of applications. In particular, deep learning CT denoising has demonstrated superior ability to reduce noise compared to conventional methods. However, the nonlinear nature of these algorithms makes it difficult to inspect and visualize how the model accomplishes the denoising task. Purpose We propose a local linearization approach to characterize and analyze the behavior of deep learning algorithms. Example analysis was performed for a classic denoising architecture with convolutional neural network and ReLU activation functions, and was extended to GELU activation and a transformer-based architecture. Methods We defined strictly local linear regions as the input space over which the activation patterns of all ReLU activation functions are the same. The extent of these regions was investigated by perturbing clinically relevant features of a lung lesion. We further defined approximately local linear regions as the input space where Jacobians are similar and linear approximation results in small error. We developed an algorithm to partition input space over a range of lesion and background features into approximately local linear regions, and separately quantified the contribution of the noise realization and anatomical background to this approximation error. The behavior of networks trained with different levels of denoising, as well as alternative architectures, was compared. Results The extent of strictly local linear regions was found to be very small. Perturbations on the scale of 10-8mm-1 were enough to push the network to a neighboring strictly local linear region. However, the Jacobians over a large number of strictly local linear regions were found to be highly similar, which suggests that the network behaves approximately as a piecewise linear system. The partitioning algorithm identified a small number of approximately local linear regions within input spaces characterized by clinically relevant features; this number was similar for the GELU variant but increased for networks trained with more aggressive noise reduction and for a transformer-based architecture, while Jacobians transferred across anatomical backgrounds also increased approximation error. Conclusions The local linearity analysis framework can be a useful tool for elucidating the behavior of neural networks that are traditionally considered as "black-boxes." Preliminary results suggest that the framework can be applied to other differentiable architectures, subject to empirical validation, to characterize these highly nonlinear, data-dependent algorithms over input spaces of interest.

title: Free-breathing fast abdominal simultaneous T 1 , T 2 , PD and B 1 mapping via deep learning reconstruction.
abstract: Background Multi-parametric quantitative MRI (mqMRI) enables non-invasive tissue characterization and holds significant clinical value in abdominal imaging. Conventional methods are restricted by long acquisition times and motion artifacts induced by physiological processes and irregular breathing, leading to registration errors between sequential acquisitions. Purpose To develop and evaluate a framework for abdominal quantitative imaging under free-breathing conditions with reduced scan time and improved robustness to motion. Methods A novel framework integrating the longitudinal magnetization-controlled multiple overlapping-echo detachment (LMC-MOLED) sequence with synthetic data-driven deep learning reconstruction was proposed. To generate the synthetic dataset for training, a respiratory motion model combining global and local displacement vector fields was developed, ensuring temporal alignment with the inter-phase intervals of LMC-MOLED acquisitions. By applying interpolation to the original template, virtual imaging objects were generated to simulate respiratory-induced deformations while preserving anatomical textures, tissue boundaries, and inter-slice correlations. These objects were subsequently processed with MRI Bloch simulation to generate the final synthetic dataset, which was used to train a BGA-Multi-UNet architecture for motion correction and improved quantitative accuracy. Results The proposed framework enabled simultaneous mapping of T 1 , T 2 , proton density, and B 1 under free-breathing conditions. With a 5-slice interleaved acquisition, the average acquisition time was reduced to approximately one second per slice without the need for respiratory gating. Both numerical and in vivo experiments demonstrated high accuracy and repeatability, with image quality comparable to conventional breath-hold acquisitions while mitigating motion-induced artifacts. Conclusion This framework offers a rapid and reliable solution for multi-parametric abdominal imaging under free-breathing conditions. The combination of synthetic motion modeling with deep learning reconstruction enables accurate quantitative mapping with effective motion correction, offering potential clinical benefits for efficient and robust abdominal magnetic resonance imaging.

title: Biological target volume and tumor spread map: A combined approach for advanced radiotherapy targeting in glioblastoma.
abstract: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) radiotherapy planning typically applies fixed margins from the Gross Tumor Volume (GTV) to define the Clinical Target Volume (CTV) and Planning Target Volume (PTV). This standardized approach ignores patient-specific patterns of microscopic tumor spread and biological abnormalities, risking under-treatment of infiltrated tissue and unnecessary exposure of healthy brain regions. Purpose To address this limitation, we extended our novel Tumor Spread (TS) mapping approach, which models microscopic infiltration along white matter tracts to generate personalized CTVs, by incorporating a Biological Target Volume (BTV), derived from advanced diffusion and perfusion MRI, into the model. We then compared three radiation treatment planning strategies: (1) GTV with standard fixed-margin CTV and PTV, (2) GTV with a personalized CTV (pCTV G ) and PTV (PTV G ), and (3) BTV with a personalized CTV (pCTV B ) and PTV (PTV B ). Each was evaluated for feasibility of dose coverage, healthy tissue sparing, and recurrence overlap. Methods MRI data from 10 newly diagnosed GBM patients were used. BTVs were contoured using Fractional Anisotropy (FA), Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC), and relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) maps. TS maps were generated from both GTV and BTV. Virtual volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) treatment plans were created for all three strategies. We compared target volumes, organ-at-risk (OAR) doses, and spatial overlap with recurrence regions identified in follow-up imaging. Results Both pCTV G and pCTV B were consistently smaller than the standard CTV, offering reduced irradiated volume while preserving tumor coverage. The pCTV G and pCTV B spared 59% and 49% of the standard CTV margin volume, respectively. All virtual plans met clinical conformality thresholds, and mean doses to organs at risk (OARs) were lower with both personalized strategies. At follow-up, 98% of the volume of recurrent tumor was included in the standard PTV, 95% in PTV G , and 97% in PTV B . Dose coverage of ≥80% was achieved in 99% of the recurrence volume with standard PTV, and in 98% with both PTV G and PTV B . Conclusion This study demonstrated the clinical feasibility and potential dosimetric benefits of MRI-derived, biology-informed personalized target volumes for radiotherapy planning of glioblastoma patients. Among the virtual personalized strategies, the approach combining the Biological Target Volume (BTV) with Tumor Spread (TS) mapping showed reduced irradiated target volume, while improving healthy tissue sparing and spatial recurrence coverage. These findings support a shift toward individualized, biology-driven radiation planning that moves beyond the traditional GTV/CTV model.

These findings support a shift toward individualized, biology-driven radiation planning that moves beyond the traditional GTV/CTV model.

title: A K-space guided invertible diffusion model for accelerating MRI reconstruction.
abstract: Background Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a core technology in clinical medical diagnosis, has long aimed to balance imaging quality and acquisition efficiency. Traditional MRI techniques, limited by the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, are faced with significant challenges in high-acceleration-factor imaging, including artifacts and detail loss due to sparse sampling. While existing parallel imaging, compressed sensing, and deep learning methods have improved reconstruction efficiency, they have limitations such as insufficient integration of electromagnetic physics models with biological tissue prior information, inadequate high-frequency information recovery, and high computational complexity. Purpose To address these persistent limitations in high-acceleration MRI reconstruction, this study proposes a K-space guided invertible diffusion model (KG-IDM) designed to improve reconstruction fidelity. Methods KG-IDM enables high-quality MRI reconstruction through Cross-domain Feature Injection (CFI) with Adaptive Channel-Spatial Interaction Attention (ACSIA) for multi-source feature alignment, and a K-space Guided Bimodal Spectral Enhancement Network (KG-BSEN) for dual-path frequency-spatial enhancement. This framework jointly exploits spatial and spectral representations, enhancing cross-domain feature consistency and reducing reconstruction artifacts. Results Experiments on the fastMRI single-coil knee dataset using retrospectively undersampled complex-valued k-space at 4× , 6× , 8× , and 10× acceleration show that KG-IDM achieves the highest mean PSNR and SSIM and the lowest mean NMSE relative to all nine baseline methods. At 4× acceleration, KG-IDM achieves 32.05 dB PSNR, 81.35% SSIM, and 0.0230 NMSE. At 10× , it achieves 25.58 dB, 62.55% , and 0.0815 , respectively. Paired volume-level Wilcoxon tests over 199 evaluation volumes showed statistically significant favorable differences in all 108 comparisons, with all Holm-adjusted p<10-4 . Conclusions By integrating measurement-guided cross-domain feature fusion with frequency-spatial refinement, KG-IDM consistently improves reconstruction fidelity across the evaluated acceleration factors and provides a promising framework for accelerated MRI reconstruction.

title: Dual-domain fusion unfolding network for compressed sensing MRI.
abstract: Background Compressed sensing magnetic resonance imaging (CS-MRI) aims to recover high-quality MRI images from undersampled k-space data. Deep unfolding networks (DUNs) have shown strong potential in CS-MRI due to their interpretability and reconstruction capability. However, existing methods still face two limitations: insufficient modeling of the complex-valued structure of MRI data and inadequate utilization of complementary k-space and image-domain information. These limitations may cause detail loss or noise artifacts in reconstructed images. Purpose This study aims to address these two challenges by developing a dual-domain unfolding framework that effectively integrates complementary information from the k-space and image domains for CS-MRI reconstruction. Methods This paper proposes a dual-domain fusion unfolding network (DDFU-Net) to address the aforementioned challenges by effectively integrating complementary information from the k-space and image domains. DDFU-Net introduces two core modules: the k-space reconstruction module (KRM) and the fusion attention module (FAM). The k-space reconstruction module processes complex-valued k-space data through real-imaginary decomposition and amplitude-phase representation modeling, with real-valued convolutional operations used for feature extraction. This design enables the network to exploit complementary information contained in the complex-valued k-space representation and improves detail recovery under high acceleration. The FAM promotes cross-domain interaction between the k-space and image-domain branches, enabling complementary feature fusion and improving detail restoration. A data consistency module is further incorporated to preserve the acquired k-space measurements during reconstruction. Results On the Brain and fastMRI datasets, DDFU-Net achieves competitive or superior reconstruction performance across the evaluated undersampling settings, with clear improvements in most comparisons. Ablation studies further validate the contribution of the major components. Conclusions The proposed DDFU-Net achieves strong reconstruction performance under different undersampling settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of the coordinated dual-domain reconstruction framework.

title: A multi-resolution SWIN transformer framework regularized by white matter time-intensity curve for brain dynamic contrast-enhanced MR image registration.
abstract: Background Deep learning-based registration methods are often computationally intensive and struggle with dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) images, as they cannot effectively distinguish motion artifacts from contrast-induced intensity variations, leading to unreliable physiological parameter estimation. Purpose To develop a novel registration framework (TIC-SViT) based on a multi-resolution SWIN transformer architecture that exploits the inherent smoothness of tissue time-intensity curves (TICs). Methods A retrospective study was conducted on DCE-MRI brain data from 59 subjects, acquired using a 3.0 T scanner with a T1-weighted spoiled gradient echo sequence. The dataset was randomly split into training (n = 4956), validation (n = 1180), and testing (n = 59) pairs. Model performance was assessed in terms of computational efficiency, registration accuracy, and clinical relevance. Comparative experiments were conducted against four representative registration approaches: the traditional optimization-based method ANTs, a CNN-based deep learning model, the groupwise multi-resolution framework (GWMS), and the transformer-based C2FViT framework. Computational efficiency was assessed by comparing parameter count, training time, and testing time per DCE-MRI case. Registration accuracy was quantified using Dice coefficient (DC) and the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) across white matter, gray matter, and cerebrospinal fluid. In addition, the temporal smoothness of TICs in arterial, venous, and white matter regions was evaluated using root mean squared error (RMSE). Clinical relevance was examined by comparing the quality of DCE-derived parameter maps generated from different registration methods. Results The proposed TIC-SViT model achieved a comparable parameter count (12.2 M, compared with 11.7, 9.5, and 12.4 M for CNN, GWMS, and C2FViT, respectively), the shortest training time and competitive testing speed (775 s and 11.7 s per case, compared with 1142 and 52.6 s for CNN, 1440 and 8.9 s for GWMS, 857 and 39.4 s for C2FViT, and 159.3 s for ANTs, which does not require training). It also produced the lowest RMSE values for TICs in artery (0.12), venous (0.14), and white matter (0.15) regions among all compared methods. In terms of global registration accuracy, C2FViT achieved the best performance, with DC values of 0.98, 0.97, and 0.82 for white matter, gray matter and cerebrospinal fluid, respectively, and the lowest HD95 value (9.5). The proposed TIC-SViT achieved the second best performance, with DC values of 0.97, 0.96, and 0.81, and HD95 of 10.2. Conclusions The proposed method demonstrated registration accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art methods, but with significant improvement in computational efficiency.

title: Development of a lung nodule volumetry tool for quality assurance assessment of low-dose lung cancer screening CT protocols.
abstract: Background Low-dose CT (LDCT) is the preferred modality for lung nodule detection and follow-up, yet standardized quality-control criteria are lacking. Volumetric accuracy is clinically important but strongly dependent on segmentation and reconstruction settings, particularly for small, low-contrast subsolid nodules, and frameworks for optimizing LDCT protocols based on volumetric performance remain limited. Purpose To develop a lung nodule segmentation and volumetry tool that evaluates volumetric accuracy across CT reconstruction settings and to demonstrate how accuracy and repeatability metrics can support protocol comparison as a quality-assurance assessment. Methods A custom semi-automatic tool was developed in Python and evaluated using the QRM Thorax phantom on a GE Revolution Apex CT system. Fifteen artificial nodules were analyzed, combining five diameters (3-12 mm) and three attenuation levels (100, -630, -800 HU). Reconstruction parameters were systematically varied, including kernel (STANDARD, LUNG), slice thickness (0.625-2.5 mm), spacing (0.625, 1.25 mm), algorithm (DLIR-H and ASiR-V at 80%), and field of view (18, 36 cm). Performance was assessed using mean relative volume error (target within ± 20%), repeatability coefficient (RC), and size-specific RMSE; the best-performing configuration per nodule type served as reference. Reconstruction effects were evaluated using factorial ANOVA, Levene's test, Welch's t-test, and bootstrap analysis with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Overall mean relative volume errors ranged from -7.1% to 6.7% for solid nodules and -14.7% to 5.8% for type 1 subsolid nodules ≥5 mm; type 2 subsolid nodules showed larger deviations (-27.1% to -12.1%). Nodule size and reconstruction kernel were the dominant contributors to mean volume error, while slice thickness and spacing mainly influenced variability. Significant differences from the reference were found for four solid-nodule settings, none for type 1, and one for type 2 subsolid settings, with degradation occurring mainly at increased slice thickness or reduced field of view. The 3 mm subsolid nodules showed consistently high variability across all settings. Conclusions The tool enabled quantitative comparison of CT reconstruction settings using volumetric accuracy and repeatability metrics. For clinically relevant sizes ( ≥5 mm), volumetric performance remained within the predefined technical-suitability range across most settings, supporting use of the tool for protocol evaluation and future dose-optimization studies.

title: Rep2Rep-Shuffle: Shuffled Repetition-to-Repetition Learning for Noise-Adaptive Self-Supervised MRI Denoising.
abstract: Purpose MRI applications with low SNR, such as non-proton imaging and low-field imaging, often require multiple signal averages to achieve adequate image quality at the cost of longer scan times. This work proposes Rep2Rep-Shuffle, a self-supervised learning framework that improves MRI denoising performance in repeated-acquisition imaging with limited training datasets. Methods Rep2Rep-Shuffle extends our previously proposed repetition-to-repetition learning (Rep2Rep)-based self-supervised denoising approach with a new shuffled repetition pairing strategy. Instead of using a fixed split between training input and target repetitions, different repetition combinations are randomly generated during training epochs for each dataset, which increases the effective training space when training datasets are limited. In addition, the framework also extends from slice-wise 2D to 3D denoising by exploiting correlations across all spatial dimensions. The proposed method was tested in vivo using sodium MRI and further validated using synthetic noisy MRI datasets. Different training strategies for both 2D and 3D denoising were compared. Results In vivo sodium MRI results demonstrated improved denoising and better preservation of anatomical structures with 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle compared with fixed pairing (Rep2Rep) and 2D denoising. Reader evaluation further confirmed that 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle received higher scores for different assessment categories. In synthetic experiments, 3D Rep2Rep-Shuffle achieved the best performance among self-supervised methods and approached the performance of supervised learning. Conclusion Rep2Rep-Shuffle outperforms Rep2Rep for MRI denoising by increasing training diversity through shuffled repetition pairing and by leveraging volumetric spatial correlations. The method is particularly suited for low-SNR MRI applications that acquire multiple repetitions but have limited training datasets.

title: Deep-Reorder: Refined Motion Correction for 3D Brain MRI via Iterative Data Regrouping.
abstract: Purpose Accurate and temporally high-resolution estimation of subject motion is paramount for effective motion-correction in MRI. This work proposes a novel approach for estimating subject motion within a 3D MRI scan with high temporal resolution. Methods Starting from an incoherent sampling scheme, images are reconstructed from temporally ordered k-space fractions via deep learning, enabling motion estimation via registration between each image. Assuming the bulk of the motion is removed using these initial estimates, the remaining misalignment between k-space fractions is expected to be minimally correlated in time. Based on this insight, an iterative strategy is proposed in which shots are arbitrarily regrouped into new k-space fractions, regardless of their original temporal ordering, for subsequent motion estimation and correction. This effectively increases the temporal resolution of the approach, enabling individual correction of all shots. Results When applied to 3D T1w TFE MRI of the brain, the proposed approach "Deep-Reorder" estimated a unique motion state for all shots, producing significantly better estimations of retrospective motion compared to estimation without iterative data regrouping. On prospectively motion-corrupted scans with intentional head movement by volunteers, the proposed approach consistently improved image quality, producing less noisy images with reduced motion artifacts. Conclusion In conclusion, the proposed approach, which is free of external tracking devices or navigators, effectively estimated 3D motion and corrected motion artifacts with increased temporal resolution.

title: Adaptive Mask-Guided k-Space Diffusion for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose Masked modeling has emerged as a powerful deep learning paradigm that reconstructs missing data by predicting masked regions, achieving strong performance across multiple domains. As a critical task in medical imaging, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction aims to recover high-quality images from under-sampled k-space data. However, existing methods usually optimize the full image domain or k-space, while overlooking the importance and structural roles of different frequency components. Methods An adaptive mask-guided diffusion model (AMDM) was developed, which leverages adaptively estimated frequency distributions from k-space to construct a hybrid mask mechanism for handling diverse k-space inputs. It enables the effective separation of high-frequency and low-frequency components, producing multiple prior representations. In addition, the frequency distribution is used to generate adaptive masks, which subsequently guide the closed-loop diffusion process. Results Experimental results demonstrated improved reconstruction performance through frequency-aware modeling. AMDM achieved a PSNR of 36.89 dB on an independent public brain dataset without retraining, even at an under-sampling factor of R=12 . Conclusion The proposed method shows that explicitly modeling k-space frequency heterogeneity provides an effective prior for MRI reconstruction, offering a promising direction for robust reconstruction under aggressive under-sampling.

Purpose

Masked modeling has emerged as a powerful deep learning paradigm that reconstructs missing data by predicting masked regions, achieving strong performance across multiple domains. As a critical task in medical imaging, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction aims to recover high-quality images from under-sampled k-space data. However, existing methods usually optimize the full image domain or k-space, while overlooking the importance and structural roles of different frequency components.

Methods

An adaptive mask-guided diffusion model (AMDM) was developed, which leverages adaptively estimated frequency distributions from k-space to construct a hybrid mask mechanism for handling diverse k-space inputs. It enables the effective separation of high-frequency and low-frequency components, producing multiple prior representations. In addition, the frequency distribution is used to generate adaptive masks, which subsequently guide the closed-loop diffusion process.

Results

Experimental results demonstrated improved reconstruction performance through frequency-aware modeling. AMDM achieved a PSNR of 36.89 dB on an independent public brain dataset without retraining, even at an under-sampling factor of R=12 .

Conclusion

The proposed method shows that explicitly modeling k-space frequency heterogeneity provides an effective prior for MRI reconstruction, offering a promising direction for robust reconstruction under aggressive under-sampling.

title: Combining Cartesian and Non-Cartesian Acceleration Techniques With SPARKLING for 1 mm Isotropic Whole-Brain MPRAGE in a Minute.
abstract: Purpose T1 -weighted MPRAGE remains a cornerstone of clinical anatomical imaging, yet its long acquisition times constrain routine use. Established acceleration techniques, namely Parallel Imaging (PI) and Compressed Sensing (CS), tend to introduce substantial noise and blurring when pushed to high acceleration factors. Although they rely on fundamentally different redundancies, combining them synergistically remains an open challenge. Methods The GoLF-SPARKLING framework was extended to jointly exploit two acceleration mechanisms: PI-based uniform undersampling in the central k-space region and variable-density CS at the periphery, with independent acceleration factors in each zone. To preserve smooth signal evolution throughout the inversion-recovery period and avoid modulation artifacts, the acquisition trajectory was reordered accordingly. The resulting method was evaluated prospectively in vivo at 1 mm isotropic resolution and benchmarked against Wave-CAIPI and Poisson-disk sampling as respective PI and CS baselines. Results The proposed hybrid approach produced sharper, less noisy, and more stable whole-brain images in approximately 1 min than either acceleration strategy alone. Purely PI-based reconstructions were degraded by high g-factor noise, while exclusively CS-based reconstructions exhibited pronounced blurring. Furthermore, this method yielded lower average volumetric errors in downstream automated brain segmentation than state-of-the-art acceleration techniques, demonstrating its clinical utility. Conclusion By jointly leveraging PI and CS, GoLF-SPARKLING achieves high acceleration factors that enable sub-minute, high-quality anatomical MRI. This translates into greater clinical throughput and more reliable imaging in patients who are challenging to scan.

title: Liver T1, T2, T2*, and PDFF Mapping at 0.55 T Using Rosette MRF With Optimized Sequence Design and Deep Image Reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose Quantitative imaging on mid-field (0.55 T) MRI systems can suffer from poor precision due to low SNR. This work presents an MRF pulse sequence optimized with Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) and combined with a multi-echo deep image prior (DIP) reconstruction for co-registered T1/T2/T2*/PDFF mapping in the liver at 0.55 T within a single breath-hold. Methods A 20 s 2D multi-echo rosette MRF breath-hold acquisition was implemented on a 0.55 T wide-bore system. The sequence design was optimized via pseudorandom search using a CRLB-based objective for T1/T2 encoding and compared with reference designs. Data were reconstructed using (i) an iterative low-rank (LR) reconstruction and (ii) a multi-echo DIP jointly modeling TR- and echo-domain dynamics including B0 effects. Water/fat separation preceded dictionary matching for T1/T2; curve fitting was used to calculate T2* and PDFF was derived from M0 with noise-bias correction. The method was evaluated in numerical simulations, NIST and fat-fraction phantom scans, and in vivo acquisitions in 10 healthy subjects. A linear mixed-effects model was used to evaluate the effects of sequence design and reconstruction method on mapping accuracy and precision. Results Optimized sequences achieved lower CRLB cost than reference designs and, in simulations, CRLB cost was correlated with T1/T2 ROI variability (R 2 = 0.76 LR; R 2 = 0.83 DIP). Phantom experiments showed agreement with reference values. In vivo, both sequence optimization and DIP reconstruction significantly reduced the standard deviation of all four parameters in liver ROIs. Conclusion CRLB-guided acquisition and multi-echo DIP reconstruction enable accurate and precise liver MRF T1/T2/T2*/PDFF mapping at 0.55 T in a single breath-hold.

title: Fast Voxelwise SNR Estimation for Iterative MRI Reconstructions.
abstract: Purpose To develop a fast, general-purpose framework for voxelwise noise characterization in iterative MRI reconstructions, recovering the image-domain noise variance, the primary quantity from which SNR, g -factor, and related image-quality metrics are derived. The framework addresses both the intractability of closed-form formulas beyond Cartesian sampling and the long runtime of pseudo multiple replica (PMR). Methods A stochastic noise estimator is proposed that operates in the image domain by Probing the Image-space noise COvariance matrix (PICO) with random probe images. Complex random-phase probes attain minimum kurtosis and reduce estimator variance in the tested reconstruction. PICO was validated against analytical benchmarks and PMR references using Cartesian knee data ( R=2 ), physical brain phantom data ( R=2,3,4 ), in vivo non-Cartesian brain data ( R=2 ), and compressed-sensing knee reconstructions ( R=2 ). Results In Cartesian reconstructions, PICO accurately reproduced analytical SENSE g -factor maps. In non-Cartesian reconstructions, it achieved 1% g -factor NRMSE ≈11.9× faster than PMR in a phantom and ≈2.81× faster in vivo, with the efficiency advantage persisting at higher acceleration. For compressed sensing, the Jacobian-based estimator produced noise maps consistent with PMR and computed them 1.84× faster at equal sample counts. Agreement worsened at large added-noise amplitudes and moderate TV strengths. Conclusion PICO targets the exact covariance of fixed linear reconstructions and a first-order covariance for nonlinear reconstructions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to PMR. By reusing existing reconstruction primitives, it could help incorporate voxelwise noise maps into reconstruction workflows.

title: FOCUS: A Frequency Offset Selection Framework for Accelerated CEST MRI Using Adaptive Subset-Level Optimization.
abstract: Purpose To develop a redundancy-aware frequency offset selection framework for accelerated chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI that reduces acquired saturation frequency offsets while preserving quantitative and classification performance. Methods FOCUS, a Frequency Offset selection framework for accelerated CEST MRI Using adaptive Subset-level optimization, was developed to account for inter-offset redundancy beyond individual offset importance. Frequency offset selection was formulated as subset-level optimization, in which candidate subsets were encoded as binary individuals and evaluated by final task performance. An artificial protozoa optimizer-based search scheme was used to explore the subset space, and a deep Q-network adaptively guided the search strategy. FOCUS was evaluated in numerical simulations, in vivo human skeletal muscle phosphocreatine quantification, and glioma molecular subtype classification, and compared with permutation importance analysis, random forest, and channel pruning. Results Under reduced frequency-offset sampling, FOCUS outperformed existing methods in both CEST quantification and glioma molecular subtype classification. For CEST quantification, FOCUS achieved the lowest root mean square error in simulations and in vivo skeletal muscle experiments, with the highest structural similarity index and peak signal-to-noise ratio in vivo. For glioma classification, FOCUS achieved the best overall performance in predicting isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation and O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase promoter methylation status. Conclusion FOCUS enables redundancy-aware frequency offset selection for accelerated CEST MRI, reducing acquired saturation frequency offsets while preserving quantitative accuracy and classification performance.

title: Quantitative Analysis of Muscle Ultrasound Images in Adult Patients With Pompe Disease Using Radiomics.
abstract: Introduction/aims Pompe disease is a genetic myopathy caused by acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme deficiency. Treatment response is mainly evaluated using motor scores, for instance the 6-min walk test (6MWT) or the Motor Function Measure-32 (MFM-32), which can be time-consuming and biased by fatigue and motivation. Quantitative muscle ultrasound may be an additional biomarker for monitoring disease progression. Our objective was to study the performance of a large number of quantitative features derived from muscle ultrasound images to predict motor involvement in late-onset Pompe disease. Methods We retrospectively collected muscle ultrasound images from 19 patients with late-onset Pompe disease and 28 control subjects, and calculated 93 quantitative features for each image. Using a radiomics approach, we selected reproducible features that were significantly different between patients and controls, and then assessed their predictive power for the 6MWT and the MFM-32 score. Results Among the 93 features, 36 (38.7%) showed good reproducibility, and 18 (19.3%) were significantly different between Pompe patients and controls after adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index. The most predictive features of motor functions were the grayscale 10th percentile in the rectus femoris, biceps brachii, deltoid, and extensor carpi radialis muscles, explaining 76% of the variance of the 6MWT, and 84% of the variance of the MFM-32 score. Discussion These findings confirm the association between muscle ultrasound and motor function in Pompe disease found by previous studies and suggest that radiomics can identify additional predictive features, such as the grayscale 10th percentile.

title: Synthetic Data in MR Spectroscopy: Current Practices, Applications, and Considerations.
abstract: Synthetic data generation has become an increasingly important component of methodological development in magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), particularly in contexts where ground-truth in vivo measurements are limited, noisy, or inaccessible. This review provides a structured overview of current practices in synthetic MRS data generation, with emphasis on the physical, biochemical, and computational assumptions that underpin commonly used models. A decomposition of synthetic MRS data is presented in terms of core building blocks, including basis sets, signal formation models, and metabolite parameter distributions such as concentration and relaxation properties. This framework is extended to advanced components required for realistic data synthesis, including baseline and nuisance signals, spatial encoding effects such as coil sensitivities and field inhomogeneities, k-space sampling and gradient imperfections, as well as sample-specific and temporal dynamics. Beyond single-voxel modeling, synthetic data generation across multiple MRS modalities is discussed, including functional MRS, diffusion-weighted MRS, and spectroscopic imaging, with emphasis on modality-specific challenges such as physiological variability, motion, and confounding signal contributions. The role of synthetic data in clinical and preclinical research, acquisition optimization, software validation, and emerging artificial intelligence applications is further examined, with particular attention to domain shift and representational realism. Current practices in validation, reporting standards, and data accessibility are also reviewed, and key gaps limiting reproducibility and interoperability across studies are identified. Overall, this work provides a unified conceptual framework for synthetic MRS data generation, clarifies underlying assumptions across modeling choices, and outlines open challenges toward improving realism, standardization, and utility in both methodological and translational applications. Conducted by the MRS Synthetic Data Working Group under the Code & Data Sharing Committee of the MRS Study Group of the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (ISMRM), this review encompasses the existing literature, supplemented by the collective experience and in-house methodologies of its contributors, providing a community perspective that extends beyond the published record.

title: Diagnostic Performance of Magnetic Resonance Elastography Versus Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography for Liver Fibrosis Staging in Steatotic Liver Disease.
abstract: Gravitational magnetic resonance elastography (GT-MRE) enables comprehensive biomechanical liver characterization and may overcome limitations of conventional elastography techniques. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) GT-MRE compared with 2D acoustic MRE (AC-MRE) and vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) for liver fibrosis staging. In this prospective study, patients with suspected or known steatotic liver disease underwent GT-MRE (2D and 3D, gradient-echo sequences) and AC-MRE (2D, spin-echo echo-planar imaging) at 1.5 T, plus VCTE with a median interval to MRE of 37 days (IQR, 20-124 days; range, 0-372 days). Statistical analyses included generalized additive models, ordinal logistic regression, and decision tree-based classification. Diagnostic performance was assessed using cumulative receiver operating characteristic analysis and corresponding areas under the curve (AUCs). Ninety-one participants (median age, 55 years [IQR, 45-64]; 41 women) were included, of whom 35 (38%) had histopathological correlation. In the biopsy-confirmed subgroup, 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising exploratory performance for early fibrosis classification. Wave attenuation achieved AUCs of 0.91 for F0 versus ≥ F1 and 0.99 for ≤ F1 versus ≥ F2, while phase angle yielded an AUC of 0.88 for F0 versus ≥ F1, with numerically higher AUCs than conventional stiffness-based metrics. For advanced fibrosis thresholds, all modalities performed well (AUC ≥ 0.84). Obuchowski measures for 3D-derived parameters were 0.95-0.96. Internally cross-validated multiparametric modeling achieved an accuracy of up to 92%. VCTE measurements plateaued beyond F3, whereas AC- and GT-MRE metrics continued to increase with fibrosis severity. 3D GT-MRE-derived viscoelastic parameters showed promising performance for liver fibrosis classification and provided biomechanical information complementary to conventional stiffness measurements. Given the limited biopsy-confirmed sample and marked class imbalance at F0, these findings require validation in larger independent cohorts before clinical implementation.

title: 2D U-Net Framework for Multiclass Automated Segmentation of Healthy Structures, Ischemic Stroke, and Glioblastoma in the Rat Brain.
abstract: Rodents are essential for preclinical brain disease research, including stroke, tumors, and neurodegenerative disorders. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables longitudinal brain tissue visualization, but accurate segmentation is crucial for meaningful analysis. This study introduces a multitask 2D U-Net, a convolutional neural network designed for automated segmentation and quantification of brain regions, ischemic stroke lesions, and tumors in rats using T 2 -weighted imaging (T 2 -wi) and T 2 -relaxation maps. The model was evaluated on the following three MRI datasets: (i) segmentation of multiple brain regions in healthy rats, (ii) ischemic stroke lesions using T 2 -relaxation maps, and (iii) glioblastoma tumors using T 2 -wi. Performance was assessed using the Dice coefficient (DC), Hausdorff distance (HD), sensitivity (SEN), and volume ratio (VR), comparing network outputs against semiautomatic ground truths and existing models. A total of 1949 images from 111 rats were analyzed, expanded to 5847 through data augmentation. After correcting an animal-level train/test partitioning that prevented data leakage between subjects, the model achieved robust accuracy across all tasks (DC = 0.80-0.96, HD = 0.83-2.16 mm, SEN = 0.75-0.96, VR = 0.89-1.10), showing a strong correlation ( ρ=0.82-0.99 ) with manual annotations. This framework improves segmentation accuracy, robustness, and applicability across different MRI settings and conditions, addressing issues like interrater variability and time inefficiency when analyzing rodent brain MRI data. Datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NOBEL-MRI/Rat-Datasets.

title: EffNetV2M-ViT: A Hybrid Deep Learning Model for MRI-Based Differentiation of Glioblastoma and Brain Metastasis.
abstract: Noninvasive differentiation between glioblastoma (GBM) and brain metastasis (BM) remains challenging because of substantial overlap in their MRI appearance. Existing deep learning (DL) approaches have primarily relied on either convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which capture local spatial features, or transformer-based models, which capture long-range contextual relationships. However, the complementary value of combining these representations for GBM-BM discrimination has not been sufficiently investigated, using independently validated multicenter data. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer (ViT) framework for automated differentiation of GBM from BM. The framework integrates EfficientNet-based convolutional feature extraction with ViT-based global feature modeling through parallel fusion. Enhancing tumor was automatically segmented using 3D U-Net, with segmentations visually reviewed and manually corrected when necessary. T2-weighted (T2W) and contrast enhanced T1-weighted (CE-T1W) MRI sequences were used as inputs. A modality ablation study was performed to identify the optimal contrast combination among T1W, CE-T1W, T2W, and FLAIR. The framework was evaluated in a retrospective cohort of 344 patients with histologically confirmed tumors using cross-validation and ensemble methods, with performance further assessed in an independent multicenter external validation cohort from different institutions, MRI scanner platforms, and patient populations. The hybrid EffNetV2M-ViT framework achieved an accuracy of 95.4%, F1-score of 96.2%, and AUC of 98.4% on the internal test set, and 90.9%, 92.7%, and 96.8% on external validation, with sensitivity, specificity of 96.2%, 93.9% and 90.5%, 91.7%, respectively. The hybrid model outperformed the standalone CNN and ViT models across both datasets, with the largest performance gains observed in the external validation cohort, support its generalizability. Ablation analysis confirmed that the paired CE-T1W + T2W input yielded the most consistent performance across both cohorts, with additional contrasts providing no added benefit. These findings suggest that combining local convolutional features with global contextual representations improves automated GBM-BM discrimination, offering a noninvasive, standardized approach for MRI-based tumor classification that may support clinical decision-making.

title: High-Resolution 3D UTE MRI for Integrated Radiation-Free Pulmonary and Osseous Thoracic Imaging.
abstract: The aim of this study is to propose a three-dimensional ultrashort echo time (3D UTE) MRI technique for integrated, radiation-free thoracic imaging and evaluate its performance for simultaneous visualization of pulmonary and osseous thoracic structures. Five volunteers were scanned on a clinical 3-T MRI system using respiratory-gated 3D UTE and zero echo time (ZTE) sequences. UTE and ZTE were compared at matched 1.6-mm isotropic resolution to assess image quality. UTE acquisitions were further performed at isotropic resolutions of 1.6, 1.4, and 1.2 mm to determine the optimal balance between spatial resolution and clinically feasible scan time. The effects of respiratory gating were evaluated by comparing gated and free-breathing acquisitions. Contrast inversion and multistructure segmentation were applied to generate CT-like bone images and 3D renderings of the lungs, rib cage, and spine. Compared with ZTE, UTE provided more homogeneous signal intensity; reduced excitation-related artifacts; and improved delineation of pulmonary vasculature, airways, and vertebral cortical bone. Increasing spatial resolution progressively improved visualization of fine pulmonary and osseous structures, with 1.2-mm isotropic resolution yielding the highest image quality while maintaining a clinically acceptable scan time of ~7 min. Respiratory gating further improved image sharpness by reducing motion-related blurring, particularly in the lungs. The optimized UTE acquisition enabled simultaneous high-resolution visualization of lung parenchyma, ribs, and spine and supported successful 3D segmentation and rendering of multiple thoracic structures from a single dataset. The proposed 3D UTE MRI enables high-resolution, simultaneous imaging of pulmonary and osseous thoracic anatomy within a single radiation-free examination. Compared with ZTE, UTE demonstrated superior image quality and structural delineation, supporting its potential as a comprehensive alternative to CT for integrated thoracic assessment.

title: The Associations Between Olfactory Bulb Morphology, Volume Change, and Olfactory Recovery.
abstract: Objective To investigate whether olfactory bulb (OB) morphology is associated with olfactory recovery following olfactory training (OT) in individuals with COVID-19-related smell loss. Study design Prospective observational study. Setting University hospital and research center. Methods Twenty women with COVID-19-associated olfactory dysfunction and 19 healthy controls underwent OT for 3 months. OB shape (oval vs non-oval) was classified using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and bilateral OB volumes were manually segmented before and after OT. Olfactory performance was assessed with the Sniffin' Sticks test. Statistical analyses included independent t tests, multimodal analysis of covariance, correlation analyses, and generalized estimating equations. Results At baseline, OB volume correlated significantly with olfactory performance. Changes in left OB volume were positively correlated with changes in odor threshold. Following OT, patients with non-oval OB shapes showed greater improvement in Threshold + Discrimination + Identification (TDI) scores and enlargement of left OB volume compared to those with oval-shaped OB. However, OB morphology did not significantly change over time in both patients and controls. Conclusion OB shape may provide a novel perspective for predicting prognosis after OT. Further studies with larger cohorts and extended training durations are warranted to validate these preliminary observations.

title: Prognostic Predictors in Patients With Necrotizing Otitis Externa: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Objective Necrotizing otitis externa (NOE) is a rare infection with a heterogeneous clinical course that complicates prognostication. The impact of diabetes mellitus on outcomes remains controversial, and objective predictors of treatment duration are unclear. This study aimed to identify the factors associated with prolonged hospitalization in patients with NOE. Study design Retrospective observational study. Setting Tertiary academic medical center. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 61 patients with NOE admitted between September 2009 and October 2024. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, microbiological, and radiological data, as well as length of hospital stay, were analyzed. Magnetic resonance imaging assessed skull-base osteomyelitis and white matter lesions using the Fazekas scale. Multivariable linear regression identified factors associated with hospital stay. Results The mean age was 70.25 ± 13.11 years (63.9% male; mean hospital stay 46.02 ± 37.50 days). Diabetes was present in 75.4% of the patients, but neither diabetes nor hemoglobin A1c levels were associated with hospital stay. In the univariate analysis, diabetic complications, external auditory canal swelling, cranial nerve palsy, peak inflammatory marker levels, inflammatory marker normalization times, and higher Fazekas scores were associated with prolonged hospitalization, whereas only diabetic complications and higher Fazekas scores remained independently associated in the multivariable analysis (adjusted R 2 = 0.425). Conclusion Diabetic complications and higher Fazekas scores were independently associated with prolonged hospitalization in patients with NOE. These findings suggest that chronic microvascular disease burden, rather than conventional vascular risk factors alone, may contribute to a prolonged disease course. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed to validate these findings.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Supraclavicular Brachiocephalic Vein Cannulation in Pediatric Patients With Hematological Disorders: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation-related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy. Aims This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound-guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure-related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients. Methods This retrospective study included 580 children (303 subclavian vein [SCV], 277 BCV) who underwent ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization between January 2021 and December 2024. We compared first-attempt success rate, overall success rate, procedural duration, intraoperative adverse events, postoperative complications, and catheter malposition. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to improve comparability between the groups with respect to measured baseline covariates. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors. Results After IPTW, the BCV approach was associated with a higher first-attempt success rate (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.05-2.81; risk difference [RD] = 0.119, 95% CI: 0.015-0.222) and a higher overall success rate (RD = 0.091, 95% CI: 0.013-0.168). The mean procedural duration was 6 min shorter in the BCV group (95% CI: -9.5 to -2.5). The BCV approach was independently associated with lower odds of intraoperative malposition (OR = 0.096, 95% CI: 0.037-0.249), postoperative malposition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.16-0.74), and perioperative complications (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.08-0.94). Multivariable regression analysis showed that catheterization approach was independently associated with catheter malposition. Conclusions Compared with SCV, ultrasound-guided BCV cannulation is associated with higher success rates, shorter procedural duration, and fewer malpositions and complications. This technique may offer particular benefits for children with hematological disorders.

title: Spatial transcriptomics reveal depth-dependent nerve growth factor and M2-like macrophage enrichment in the perineural invasion of distal cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a frequent pathological feature of distal cholangiocarcinoma. The spatial molecular programs associated with PNI are unclear. We aimed to characterize tumor-nerve-immune interactions linked to PNI using spatial transcriptomics and independent validation. Spatial transcriptomics was performed using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiler on six cases of surgically resected distal cholangiocarcinoma (non-PNI, n = 3; PNI, n = 3). Regions of interest included non-PNI tumor regions, surface mucosal tumor regions without neural contact (PNI-surface), and tumor regions adjacent to S100-positive nerves (PNI-perineural). Tumor compartments were enriched by CK19-based segmentation. Differential expression and pathway analyses were performed using iDEP/DESeq2 and Reactome/Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment. Validation at the protein level was conducted using immunohistochemistry in an independent cohort (non-PNI, n = 22 and PNI, n = 82) for nerve growth factor (NGF), CD68, and CD163. Three-dimensional nerve architecture was assessed in nine additional cases using tissue clearing. PNI-associated compartments and non-PNI regions had distinct transcriptional profiles. Compared to that in non-PNI, 109 genes were differentially expressed in PNI-surface (34 up- and 75 downregulated) and 179 in PNI-perineural (64 up- and 115 downregulated). Pathway analyses identified enrichment of immune-, microenvironment-, and neurotrophic-related programs, including NGF-associated signatures. Tumor-cell NGF expression was significantly higher in PNI-positive tumors (median H-score: 215 versus 119, p < 0.0001) and increased with depth in PNI cases (p < 0.0001). Deep invasive regions of PNI-positive tumors saw a significant increase in CD68-positive (median 313 versus 210 cells per high-power field, p < 0.001) and CD163-positive (median 64 versus 40 cells per high-power field, p < 0.01) macrophages. CD163/CD68 ratio increased in deep versus surface regions, specifically in PNI-positive tumors (p < 0.0001). PNI-positive distal cholangiocarcinoma exhibited spatially distinct tumor programs and depth-dependent remodeling involving NGF upregulation and M2-like macrophage enrichment, identifying potential therapeutic targets. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Modernizing reporting and communication of isolated echogenic intracardiac foci and choroid plexus cysts in the cell-free DNA era.
abstract: Echogenic intracardiac foci and choroid plexus cysts are among the most common findings on second-trimester prenatal ultrasound. Historically classified as "soft markers," they were incorporated into aneuploidy risk assessment in an era when screening relied on maternal age and serum analytes with limited performance. The widespread adoption of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening has fundamentally altered this paradigm. With detection rates exceeding 99% for trisomy 21, the modest likelihood ratios associated with isolated EIF and CPC no longer meaningfully alter post-test probability or clinical management. These findings are therefore best regarded as common normal variants rather than clinically significant markers of aneuploidy. Despite this transformation in prenatal screening, reporting and communication practices have changed little and remain highly variable, often influenced by historical practice patterns and medicolegal concerns rather than contemporary evidence. Numerous studies demonstrate that disclosure of isolated EIF and CPC may result in maternal anxiety, persistent concern despite reassurance, unnecessary diagnostic testing, and disruption of maternal-fetal bonding. These effects may be amplified by immediate patient access to ultrasound reports and terminology that continues to imply pathology where none exists. This review examines the historical and contemporary evidence supporting a modernized approach to the reporting and communication of isolated EIF and CPC in the era of cfDNA screening and proposes an evidence-based framework for clinical practice. In pregnancies with low-risk cfDNA results and a normal detailed fetal anatomic survey, isolated EIF and CPCs should be regarded as benign findings without clinical significance. Contemporary evidence no longer supports the routine reporting and communication of these findings in the context of aneuploidy risk. When disclosure occurs, communication should be non-alarmist, emphasize that these are normal variants, and avoid terminology suggesting increased risk for chromosomal abnormalities. Aligning reporting and communication with current evidence has the potential to reduce patient harm while promoting patient-centered prenatal care.

title: Observing Skepticism Toward a Breast Cancer Screening Decision Aid Over Time.
abstract: Objective Prior research reported that some women are skeptical toward messages about mammography screening evidence, particularly information about overdiagnosis and false positives. The proposed cause of skepticism is that the evidence is surprising and different from other screening messages, a finding which suggests that skepticism might decline as the information becomes more familiar. The present research tested the hypothesis that skepticism declines over time with repeated exposure, and sought to replicate prior evidence for the antecedents of observed skepticism. Methods This longitudinal study recruited women ages 39-49 from two health systems. Women received a decision aid (DA) communicating mammography screening evidence prior to an annual well visit. Skepticism toward the DA information was measured immediately after the DA, after the clinic visit, and 3 months later. Hypothesis-relevant predictors of skepticism were assessed. Results Skepticism was greater toward information about overdiagnosis and false positives compared to benefits, and skepticism was greater among participants who felt the evidence conflicted with past screening messages. We also observed that higher breast cancer anxiety was associated skepticism toward screening harms. Moreover, contrary to predictions, two facets of skepticism-reactance and disbelief-increased over time. Exploratory post hoc analyses suggested that increases in skepticism were associated with participants' perceptions that the DA conflicted with their doctors' screening message. Conclusions Some people express skepticism toward mammography evidence, and these feelings are associated with perceived conflicting messages and cancer anxiety. Skepticism may not decline over time if messages from other sources conflict with the DA information. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov registration NCT05838417.

title: Informing Ambulatory Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Study Design Using Models Bridging Timed Function Tests and Fat Fraction Imaging Biomarkers.
abstract: This study aimed to inform the use of magnetic resonance (MR) imaging biomarkers in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) clinical trials by quantifying longitudinal associations between timed function tests (TFTs) (i.e., the 10-m walk/run (TMW), supine-to-stand (STS), and climb 4 stairs (CFS)) and fat fraction (FF) measures from two leg muscles (i.e., the soleus (SOL) and vastus lateralis (VL)). Additionally, this study aimed to identify sensitive age ranges and clinically relevant covariate effects for these measures. Six multivariate disease progression models were developed using natural history data from the ImagingNMD study (NCT01484678) and validated with data from investigational clinical trials, employing Bayesian nonlinear mixed-effects modeling in Monolix (ver. 2023R1). A sigmoid Emax function and a multiplication of Chapman-Richards growth and sigmoid I max function best captured the longitudinal dynamics of FF and TFT measures, respectively. The population distributions of the simulated ages at which the measures reach half of their maximum change ( DPT50 ), peaked at 12.8, 10.6, and 11.4 years for TMW, STS, and CFS velocity, respectively, and 12.4 and 10.9 years for FF-SOL and FF-VL. Steroid use delayed DPT50 of STS and CFS velocities and FF-SOL. Baseline endpoint values robustly predicted individualized trajectories for STS velocity (for all ages) and FF-VL (in older baseline age groups), but not for other measures. Older baseline age groups showed consistent DPT50 predictions across models. The established multivariate models can serve as informative tools for biomarker selection and refinement of inclusion/exclusion criteria in DMD clinical trials.

title: Thoracic Endometriosis Mimicking a Lung Mass: Management With Single-Stage Biopsy and Microwave Ablation.
abstract: Thoracic endometriosis syndrome is a rare extrapelvic manifestation involving the pleura, diaphragm or lung parenchyma. Presentation as a solitary pulmonary nodule mimicking malignancy is uncommon. We report a 31-year-old asymptomatic woman with an enlarging right lower lobe nodule, measuring 1.8-2.1 cm over 3 months. Following shared decision-making, single-stage image-guided biopsy and microwave ablation (MWA) were performed. Histopathology confirmed pulmonary endometriosis. No clinically significant postoperative complications occurred, and the patient was discharged on postoperative Day 1. Follow-up CT at 6 and 12 months demonstrated no obvious local recurrence without additional treatment. This case describes a potential minimally invasive approach for selected pulmonary lesions, although the safety, efficacy and long-term outcomes of MWA for pulmonary endometriosis remain uncertain.

title: Primary Mediastinal Kaposiform Hemangioendothelioma Involving the Superior Vena Cava in an Adult: An Extremely Rare Entity.
abstract: Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare vascular tumour predominantly affecting infants. Primary mediastinal involvement in adults is exceptionally rare. We report a rare adult case mimicking thymoma but involving the superior vena cava (SVC). A 29-year-old male presented with an anterior mediastinal mass suspected as thymoma. Imaging revealed a solid lesion and the patient underwent surgical resection via median sternotomy. Intraoperatively, the tumour showed dense adherence to the SVC, necessitating SVC plasty. Histopathology confirmed KHE. The patient recovered uneventfully. Although KHE is primarily a paediatric diagnosis, it must be considered in the differential diagnosis of adult anterior mediastinal masses. Complete surgical resection remains the treatment of choice, though vascular reconstruction may be required due to the tumour's infiltrative nature.

title: Diagnostic Challenges in Paediatric Pulmonary Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Paediatric lung nodules pose a diagnostic challenge due to a broad differential diagnosis and limited standardized evaluation guidelines. We present the case of a 12-year-old female with an incidentally discovered 27 mm calcified left pulmonary nodule during evaluation for chronic cough. She was asymptomatic at presentation, with an unremarkable examination and an extensive negative infectious, oncologic, and rheumatologic workup. Procedural challenges due to the proximity to the airway hilum, along with limited access to paediatric bronchoscopic expertise, necessitated multi-institutional coordination for surgical biopsy. Histopathology confirmed pulmonary mucoepidermoid carcinoma (PMEC), followed by lobectomy with negative margins and an excellent prognosis. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of paediatric lung nodules and the importance of multidisciplinary and cross-institutional coordination when procedural feasibility and specialized expertise limit diagnostic approach.

title: Tunable 18 F-Labeling of Erlotinib-Based Small Molecule Nanodrugs for Rapid PET Imaging and Targeted Therapy.
abstract: Small molecule nanodrugs (SMNs) offer unique advantages for cancer therapy, yet accurately tracking their in vivo fate without perturbing their native assembly remains challenging. Here, we report a spacer engineering strategy that enables efficient 1 8 F-labeling while preserving SMNs self-assembly. Erlotinib-based amphiphilic derivatives containing oligoethylene glycol (OEG) spacers of tunable length were designed to simultaneously regulate steric hindrance for aliphatic S N 2 radiofluorination and the amphiphilic balance required for nanoparticle formation. Spacer elongation reduced steric hindrance at the labeling site and thereby improved radiochemical yields, while also enabling precise control over nanoparticle size. The optimized radiolabeled formulation, [ 18 F]E3F NPs , exhibited prolonged blood circulation and rapid tumor accumulation, enabling high-contrast PET imaging of PANC-1 xenografts as early as 15 min after injection. In addition, the corresponding nonradioactive formulation, E3F NPs , showed significantly improved antitumor efficacy compared with nonassembled E3F through reduced EGFR phosphorylation and increased tumor cell apoptosis. This work provides an initial evaluation that spacer engineering can coordinate radiolabeling and self-assembly while enabling PET tracking of SMNs, supporting the development of image-guided cancer theranostics.

title: Outcomes of fetuses undergoing vesicoamniotic shunting for lower urinary tract obstruction: systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Objective To report the outcomes of fetuses undergoing vesicoamniotic shunting for lower urinary tract obstruction (LUTO). Methods MEDLINE and EMBASE databases were searched electronically from inception to 15 January 2025. The inclusion criteria were studies reporting the outcome of fetuses with isolated LUTO, defined as LUTO with no additional structural anomalies detected at the time of diagnosis, that underwent vesicoamniotic shunt placement. The outcomes observed included: overall fetal loss, defined as miscarriage or intrauterine fetal demise; neonatal death (NND); oligohydramnios at the time of diagnosis; additional structural anomaly detected on follow-up ultrasound assessment after shunt insertion; oligohydramnios at follow-up ultrasound assessment; preterm birth (PTB) < 37, < 32 and < 28 weeks' gestation; preterm prelabor rupture of membranes; shunt dislocation; shunt occlusion; need for shunt reinsertion; pulmonary hypoplasia at birth; abnormal renal function at birth and at pediatric follow-up assessment; need for dialysis; and need for renal transplant. All outcomes were explored in the overall population of fetuses with isolated LUTO. Furthermore, we performed subgroup analyses of fetuses that presented with a normal amniotic fluid volume before shunt placement, those that underwent shunting in the first trimester and analysis according to the type of vesicoamniotic shunt (double pigtail or double basket) used. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was used to combine data, and results are reported as pooled proportions with 95% CI. Results Overall, 17 studies were included in the systematic review and 15 in the meta-analysis. Overall fetal loss occurred in 10.0% (95% CI, 5.1-16.3%) of fetuses with a prenatal diagnosis of LUTO, and NND occurred in 15.8% (95% CI, 9.5-23.4%). PTB < 37, < 32 and < 28 weeks occurred in 63.3% (95% CI, 43.2-78.1%), 24.8% (95% CI, 12.3-40.0%) and 6.0% (95% CI, 0.4-17.1%) of cases, respectively. Shunt dislocation was reported in 37.2% (95% CI, 24.5-48.5%) of cases. At the follow-up ultrasound scan after shunt insertion, oligohydramnios was reported in 46.4% (95% CI, 27.6-65.7%) of cases. Abnormal renal function at birth and at pediatric follow-up were reported in 53.9% (95% CI, 35.6-71.6%) and 56.0% (95% CI, 39.0-72.4%) of cases, respectively. When considering studies reporting the outcome of fetuses that underwent shunt insertion for LUTO with normal amniotic fluid volume at the time of diagnosis, overall fetal loss occurred in 6.4% (95% CI, 2.6-11.7%) and NND occurred in 10.2% (95% CI, 4.6-17.8%) of cases, while abnormal renal function at birth and at pediatric follow-up assessment were reported in 26.9% (95% CI, 10.4-47.7%) and 28.9% (95% CI, 17.8-41.4%) of cases, respectively. In fetuses that underwent vesicoamniotic shunting in the first trimester (< 14 weeks), the incidence of abnormal renal function at birth was 18.6% (95% CI, 0.5-54.0%). When considering different types of shunt, shunt dislocation was reported in 41.4% (95% CI, 25.7-58.1%) of fetuses with a double-pigtail shunt and 30.3% (95% CI, 19.7-42.0%) of fetuses with a double-basket shunt. Conclusions There is limited evidence on the role of vesicoamniotic shunting in fetuses with LUTO. There was a high observed rate of shunt dislocation and abnormal renal function after birth. Further evidence is needed to elucidate whether the risk of adverse outcome is lower in fetuses presenting with normal amniotic fluid volume before shunt insertion and in those undergoing placement of a double-basket shunt compared with a double-pigtail shunt, as the design of the included studies did not allow us to perform a direct comparison. © 2026 The Author(s). The outcomes observed included: overall fetal loss, defined as miscarriage or intrauterine fetal demise; neonatal death (NND); oligohydramnios at the time of diagnosis; additional structural anomaly detected on follow-up ultrasound assessment after shunt insertion; oligohydramnios at follow-up ultrasound assessment; preterm birth (PTB) < 37, < 32 and < 28 weeks' gestation; preterm prelabor rupture of membranes; shunt dislocation; shunt occlusion; need for shunt reinsertion; pulmonary hypoplasia at birth; abnormal renal function at birth and at pediatric follow-up assessment; need for dialysis; and need for renal transplant. All outcomes were explored in the overall population of fetuses with isolated LUTO. Furthermore, we performed subgroup analyses of fetuses that presented with a normal amniotic fluid volume before shunt placement, those that underwent shunting in the first trimester and analysis according to the type of vesicoamniotic shunt (double pigtail or double basket) used. Random-effects meta-analysis of proportions was used to combine data, and results are reported as pooled proportions with 95% CI.

Results

Overall, 17 studies were included in the systematic review and 15 in the meta-analysis. Overall fetal loss occurred in 10.0% (95% CI, 5.1-16.3%) of fetuses with a prenatal diagnosis of LUTO, and NND occurred in 15.8% (95% CI, 9.5-23.4%). PTB < 37, < 32 and < 28 weeks occurred in 63.3% (95% CI, 43.2-78.1%), 24.8% (95% CI, 12.3-40.0%) and 6.0% (95% CI, 0.4-17.1%) of cases, respectively. Shunt dislocation was reported in 37.2% (95% CI, 24.5-48.5%) of cases. At the follow-up ultrasound scan after shunt insertion, oligohydramnios was reported in 46.4% (95% CI, 27.6-65.7%) of cases. Abnormal renal function at birth and at pediatric follow-up were reported in 53.9% (95% CI, 35.6-71.6%) and 56.0% (95% CI, 39.0-72.4%) of cases, respectively. When considering studies reporting the outcome of fetuses that underwent shunt insertion for LUTO with normal amniotic fluid volume at the time of diagnosis, overall fetal loss occurred in 6.4% (95% CI, 2.6-11.7%) and NND occurred in 10.2% (95% CI, 4.6-17.8%) of cases, while abnormal renal function at birth and at pediatric follow-up assessment were reported in 26.9% (95% CI, 10.4-47.7%) and 28.9% (95% CI, 17.8-41.4%) of cases, respectively. In fetuses that underwent vesicoamniotic shunting in the first trimester (< 14 weeks), the incidence of abnormal renal function at birth was 18.6% (95% CI, 0.5-54.0%). When considering different types of shunt, shunt dislocation was reported in 41.4% (95% CI, 25.7-58.1%) of fetuses with a double-pigtail shunt and 30.3% (95% CI, 19.7-42.0%) of fetuses with a double-basket shunt.

Conclusions

There is limited evidence on the role of vesicoamniotic shunting in fetuses with LUTO. There was a high observed rate of shunt dislocation and abnormal renal function after birth. Further evidence is needed to elucidate whether the risk of adverse outcome is lower in fetuses presenting with normal amniotic fluid volume before shunt insertion and in those undergoing placement of a double-basket shunt compared with a double-pigtail shunt, as the design of the included studies did not allow us to perform a direct comparison. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Classification of brain variants on fetal ultrasound: international Delphi consensus.
abstract: Objective To develop an expert consensus classification and management framework for fetal-brain variants identified on prenatal ultrasound across all trimesters of pregnancy that cannot be categorized confidently as either benign or pathological. Methods A two-round international Delphi survey was conducted among experts in fetal medicine and neurosonography, with survey data collected between September 2025 and March 2026. Forty-eight fetal-brain variants, identified through a scoping literature review of PubMed/MEDLINE from database inception to August 2025, performed between June and August 2025, and illustrated with representative ultrasound images, were evaluated. Brain variants were classified according to clinical significance and recommended management into three predefined categories: 'green' (benign variants requiring no additional investigation or follow-up), 'orange' (requiring neurosonographic follow-up) and 'red' (requiring dedicated neurosonography, fetal-brain magnetic resonance imaging and/or genetic investigations). Consensus was predefined as ≥ 70% agreement. In Round 2, experts confirmed their agreement regarding categorization of variants that had reached consensus in Round 1 and reassessed variants that did not reach initial consensus. Results Forty-eight experts from 14 countries participated in Round 1 and 39 (81.3%) completed both rounds. Of the 48 evaluated variants, 35 (72.9%) reached consensus after two rounds: 12 were classified as 'green', seven as 'orange' and 16 as 'red'. Green variants included isolated choroid plexus cysts < 10 mm across all trimesters, regular asymmetry of the choroid plexuses, isolated cavum septations, cavum vergae, cavum velum interpositum, isolated small cavum septi pellucidi with intact corpus callosum and dolichocephaly with normal head circumference and normal brain morphology. Orange variants included isolated enlargement of intracranial translucency with preserved anatomy, large or bilateral choroid plexus cysts, isolated enlargement of subarachnoid spaces without compression and isolated cyst of the cavum septi pellucidi. Red variants included abnormal posterior fossa markers (loss of normal three-space anatomy, increased brainstem-vermis angle, reduced brainstem-occipital bone distance), periventricular cysts associated with adjacent white-matter abnormalities, thickened corpus callosum and distortion of the interhemispheric fissure, among other findings. Thirteen (27.1%) variants failed to reach consensus, highlighting persistent uncertainty in interpreting subtle isolated asymmetries and selected cystic variants. Conclusions This international Delphi consensus proposes an initial expert-derived classification of commonly encountered feta-brain variants on ultrasound. Because the classification has not been validated against postnatal imaging or neurodevelopmental outcomes and reproducibility has not been assessed, prospective evaluation is required before it can be applied in routine practice. © 2026 International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology.
